# R21 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 10 September 1588: the King dismisses his ministers)

Translation of `R21_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 94r] […] Our Lord: the resolution taken by His Majesty to remove at one and the same time all his secretaries of
state, the Chancellor and Monsieur de Bellièvre, with some other officers, has thrown the whole court into great
suspicion and talk; and as His Majesty has given no reason that moved him to so sudden a change, everyone reasons
according to his own sense, and few are those who praise this deed, with which Monsieur de Guise shows himself little
satisfied, since it seems to him that His Majesty's not having communicated anything to him on this matter is a clear
sign that he has little confidence in him. The same happens with the Queen Mother, with whom, they say, His Majesty no
more wanted to take counsel in this case; and she shows, at least in appearance, that she resents it greatly, because
most of these men had been brought into their offices by her in the time of the minority of the Kings her sons. All
the same I am assured that, on leaving Chartres, the King communicated this plan of his to Her Majesty, a plan that
[had] its origin in his mind from the time he left Paris because of the revolt of this [f. 94v] city, as he then
thought he had found in these men little secrecy, not to say loyalty. All the rest of the court also shows displeasure,
and many have begun to fear that the same may happen to them as has happened to these, because the change happened the
same day. And I went to the audience of His Majesty I took the occasion to ask him whether what I had heard of this change was
true. He answered that it was most true. And I told him that, although all that His Majesty did ought to be counselled
with great prudence and settled with mature deliberation, I, with the affection I bore to his service and to the
universal good of the whole kingdom, wished to say that this resolution was of the greatest importance, since His
Majesty was depriving himself at one stroke of all those who understand the true state of his affairs, to bring new
men into the government; and even were they the best in the world, they would still have to learn at his cost the way
to serve him well, and only with difficulty and after a long time could they reach the perfection that these others,
by their [f. 95r] own worth, being most excellent men and with long experience, had already acquired; and that it
seemed to me that, these men having full knowledge of his every secret thought and knowing where every weakness of this
kingdom lies, they could do him great harm if, ruled by indignation, they let themselves be persuaded to join His
Majesty's enemies; adding various other reasons that then came to my mind, which it would be too long to relate in
full. His Majesty answered that he did not think these men were of so bad a condition as to turn against him; they were
all rich and would be glad to enjoy in peace the many goods they had acquired in his service; and he wanted to learn
from Our Lord, who made himself obeyed and feared by everyone — as he said he had just been reading a letter from his
ambassador resident with Our Lord, in which, by order of Our Lord, he wrote to him that he too should make himself
obeyed and feared by his ministers and his subjects; that he was now 37 years old, and wanted from now on to attend
unweariedly [f. 95v] to the government of his kingdom, and to see whether, governing in his own way, he could bring
things to a better state than he had done with the counsel of these men; of whom he said that, had he not removed them
now, it would easily have happened that the assembly of the Estates itself would have asked for them to be removed
from the council, because they had been the instruments of putting forward many [courses] that have caused great harm
in the kingdom and the worst dissatisfaction among the people. I praised His Majesty's wish to make use of the […]
fatherly counsels of Our Lord, assuring him that, if he did so, it would put his affairs in a [state] […] better than
they are; but that I did not see Our Lord advising him, in a time of such need as this, to deprive himself at a single
blow of all the ministers who know his secrets, and that this was a dangerous act and would give the whole world much
to talk about; that if he would have it so, he should at least try, since he did not show that he had any fault
against them worthy of punishment, to keep them in his [f. 96r] devotion, so that they do not take another side, as
Monsieur du Ferrier did, who, not being esteemed by him, became chancellor of the present King of Navarre. His Majesty
told me that he was quite disposed to do this, and that in effect he would hold them under his protection against
anyone who wanted to offend [them], but that he no longer wanted to use [them], being resolved to have people who serve
him in his way, and not like these, who served him in theirs. After this conversation His Majesty went on to thank me
for the good offices I had done with Monsieur d'Épernon and with the abbé del Bene to keep him in his devotion, and
told me that he had sent his physician back to the said Épernon to see whether he could bring him to give up Boulogne
and Metz, [for] he would then be content to leave him all the rest of the governments he holds; but from what I hear on
the other side, it seems to me that he shows himself most resolved not to do it, and it is much feared that he may
join Montmorency and Navarre. Although His Majesty does not believe it, thinking that he, so as not to lose the 400
[f. 96v] thousand scudi he finds he has on the salt farm, will not abandon his side. I do not fail to do what I can,
both with the said Épernon and with the King and the Duke of Guise, to see that this man is kept on the side of the
Catholics, judging that this is of the greatest importance because of the large forces in his hands; and he quite often
gives me firm assurance of it in his letters, showing the greatest desire that Our Lord should remain well satisfied
of his actions, for which reason he still says he wants to send a man to Our Lord. […]

R22, Francia 22/5, n.d. [Sept 1588] (duplicate)

Replies to Montalto. Morosini has kept pressing for the council; the Estates promise to ask for it. His faculties will not be obeyed unless the Parlement verifies them.

# R22 — Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 7 October 1588: the Council of Trent, the legate's faculties, the Count of Soissons' absolution, the vice-legate of Avignon and Épernon (Francia 22/5, ff. 132r–135v)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1690 (KaJo, March 2016; the first line is marked "dup." in clear, a
duplicate) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py`
(`R22_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, for one figure
in question, on the DECODE image (`R22_corrections.tsv`). Date and place from the covering letter in clear on the
DECODE "cleartext" images (D948–949: "Di Bles il 7 di ottobre 1588", answering Montalto's letters of 19 September
"con l'altro cifra"); the cipher itself cites "lettere di V. S. Ill.ma di 19 del pasato". No contemporary decipherment
on the images; Rome's decipherments (Francia 27) are not imaged. Tempesti, *Vita di Sisto V* (1754) II, tells the
Soissons absolution and the faculties affair in outline only; not used for words.
The text breaks off at the foot of 135v in mid-sentence ("quello dela …"): the last leaf of the cipher is not among
the DECODE images.
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants; "comonicare", "condesendere", "Suisone" for Soissons);
punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 129 duca di,
131 cardinale di, 135 uescoui, 151 Francia, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 195 Auignone,
213 ambasciatore, 217 corriere, 219 cifra, 221 lettere, 226 catolici, 119 Regina d'Inghilterra, 123 Re di Dania);
m + 8 = -mente. Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [x] supplied.

## Reading

[f. 132r] Questo […] al foglio di cifra uenuto nele lettere di V. S. Ill.ma di 19 del pasato […] non ocore dire, che
quanto ala publicatione del concilio di Trento io non ho mai tralasciato di fare ogni eficacisimo oficio perché sia
liberam[ente] et senza alcuna conditione publicato, come anco con diuerse mie lettere ne ho dato conto a V. S. Ill.ma;
et già ho hauto promesa da tuti tre li Stati, se bene separatam[ente] l'uno dal altro, che tuti insieme lo dimandarano
nei loro capito[li] a S. M.tà. Non lasarò di continouare, seruendomi di quelle persuasioni che sono esprese nela deta
cifra. Quanto a presentare le facoltà dela legatione al parlamento, scrisi già a V. S. Ill.ma con mie di 12 del pasato
di hauerle presentate […], così consigliato da persone molto principali et deuotisimi di N. S. et di cotesta Santa
Sede. S. M.tà tutauia le tiene apreso di sé, non hau[en]do hauto tempo di uederle et considerarle; io non mancarò di
fare quanto oficio che […] mi comete. Ma è da sapere che se le […] facoltà non sono uerificate dal parlamento, che tuti
gli ati che io facesi sariano [f. 132v] senza anima […], esendo il parlam[ento] quello che ha da farli esequire et
ubidire, come anco sucede di tuti li editi et ordini che fa il Re medesmo; che se non sono uerificati dal parlamento
non uengono ubiditi, portando così la forma del gouerno di questo regno.

Quanto ala asolutione dei principi di Uandomo, hauendo ueduto quello che V. S. Ill.ma mi scriue fuori di cifra con più
sue, che deba in ogni modo [?aspetare] altro ordine prima che uenire ad esa asolut[i]one, et considerato poi quello che
si contiene in esa cifra, io non ho saputo pigliare partito; perché se bene mi dice di mandarmi la facoltà et il modo
di asoluerli, et che io, secondo che mi parerà bene, la esequisca o la ritardi, come giudicarò esere bene del regno,
con tuto che pensasi di potere dar hora in uigore di questo ordine la asolutione, non ho però creduto poter alterare il
modo che la mi manda; del quale non si uolendo a modo alcuno contentare il conte di Suisone, dicendo che non si deue
acusare [f. 133r] di pecato che non ha pure pensato, non che comeso, ho risoluto di diferire, se bene con grandisimo
risentimento così del conte sodeto come di tuti i suoi et del Re medesmo; ma, amando io più tosto di ubidire
precisem[ente] ali ordini di N. S. che di sodisfare ad altri, ho creduto non potere pasare più oltre la loro querela.
[…] che, hauendole io fato intendere […], come V. S. Ill.ma mi scrise con le sue di 22 d'agosto, et io con mie di 2
del pasato auisai V. S. Ill.ma di hauere comonicato questo […] le loro Maiestà et con li ilustrisimi di Borbone et di
Uandomo, sopra di che haueuano tratato meco dela forma del[a] asolutione, et fato condesendere il sodeto conte a
contentarsi di abiurare nela forma che uedrà V. S. Ill.ma per la copia che le mando, nela quale è narrato la uerità del
fato et posta la sostanza di quello; et a me è parso che più importase leuando quelle parole [f. 133v] che ofendeuano
questi signori. Et il giorno medesmo che mi capitorono le lettere di V. S. Ill.ma io doueuo dargli la asolutione,
esendosi ordinato che, giungendo il conte in breue […] andase altroue, uenise a smontare ala casa dela mia
habitatione, doue con le debite circonstanze si saria fato l'uficio. Però, esendosi partito di casa sua et condoto a
due leghe uicino a qui, g[l]i pareua di riceuere grande afronto se io non [l']asolueuo. Io mi sono scusato con dire […]
di non potere fare dauantagio di quello che mi [?uiene] comandato, et [che] N. S. ama il sig. conte di Suisone et
gli darà in ogni modo la sodeta asolutione, ma che, hauendo sua Ecel. mandato un gentilomo a N. S. per questo efeto,
[…] mandarà quello ordine che le parerà a proposito. Il che inteso, dai sig. cardinali di Borbone et di Uandomo uenero
subito a ritrouarmi, facendomi grande instanza a uolerli compiacere del[a] asolutione; et io, dapoi hauere ueduto che
non si [f. 134r] contentauano dela forma mandata da V. S. Ill.ma, risposi a le loro sig. ilustris. in conformità di
quello haueuo deto prima; onde si risolsero di andare a ritrouare il Re, con il quale hano fato gagliardisimo oficio
perché S. M.tà spedisca […] in diligenza a Roma per questo rispeto. Et hora mi uengono a dire che il corriere partirà
fra due hore; però io scriuo la presente in molta freta, ma non uoglio lasar di dirle che qui mostrano di sapere che
questa mutatione [?procede] per mali ofici che siano stati fati con N. S. ad instanza del sig. cardinale di Sans, dal
ilustris. Alesandrino, et si lamentano di [?me], che io li habi esortati a mandare un huomo espreso a N. S., poi che
molti uescoui in Francia haueuano autorità di asoluerli senza andare a Roma. Io, per quello che conosco et sono
informato, truouo che il conte di Suisone non ha più di 20 anni, et che quando fu dato al sig. cardinale di Borbone non
haueua più di 4 anni, et dapoi è stato educato da sua Sig. ilustris. et uisuto sempre catolico, et hora si mostra
[f. 134v] afetionatis. ala religione catolica; et temo che il metere dificoltà nel'asolutione non posi giouare né ala
religione catolica né al regno, perché questo al sicuro renderà più dificile il ritorno del Nauarro al'obedienza dela
Sede apostolica, et sarà causa di rinouare l'odio fra questo Re et quelli di Guisa, poi che tengono per certo che tuto
il male uenga da loro, se bene al presente, per ofici fati anco da me, si mostrano insieme asai bene disposti. Pare
anco che il Re di ciò se ne risenti molto, et che uoglia diferire sino al ritorno di questo […] il dare principio ali
Stati; ma [?con] me S. M.tà non ne ha ancora parlato, non hauendo potuto andare a ritrouarla per hauermi fato male a un
piede, che non mi permete di poter caminare. Spero fra uno o duo giorni poter uscire, il che desidero somam[ente] per
certificarmi se è uero che quello ambasciatore del Re di Dania, che fuori di cifra scriuo esere uenuto a questa corte,
uenga per persuadere S. M.tà di unirsi con il suo Re a difesa dela Regina d'Inghilterra, per fare in [f. 135r] tal caso
quello oficio che sarà conueniente per [h]onore del sig. Dio et seruitio di N. S.

Mi sono molto marauigliato che mons. uicelegato di Auignone si dolga, come V. S. Ill.ma mi scriue nela sodeta cifra,
che, hauendomi lui scrito più uolte per cose importanti al suo gouerno, io non gli habi risposto; il che quando fose
uero, con gran [r]agione V. S. Ill.ma potria dire che questo non piace a N. S. Ma la deue restare sicura che io non ho
hauto dal sodeto mons. […] che tre lettere sole di qualche negotio, ale quali tute non solo ho risposto con lettere,
ma anco con tuti quelli efeti che posino uenire da me, come benisimo lo ha il Fiorauanti, secretario suo, che da molti
mesi in qua se ne sta in corte tratando negoti del uicelegato senza comonicare meco se non quello che li torna a comodo.
Il medesmo poso dire al'ultimo capo dela sodeta cifra, doue mi dice che il duca di Epernone et la Ualeta suo fratelo si
dolgono di esere abandonati da cotesta Santa Sede, et che N. S. si marauiglia che io per questi signori [f. 135v] non
habi fato l'uficio conueniente, come mi è stato scrito per lettere famigliari, per breui et per instrutioni; et mi
consolo che V. S. Ill.ma nela terza lettera sua dela medesima data di 19 de[l] pasato, fuori di cifra, mi scriue che
l'oficio fato da […] p[e]l duca di Guisa per beneficio di Epernone et del fratelo, et le lettere scrite loro, siano
piaciute a N. S., et uole che si camini inanzi in questo negotio. Però prego V. S. Ill.ma di asicurare N. S. che io non
lasarò mai di ubidire con ogni pronteza ali o[r]dini di N. S., né temo che haurà mai causa di tenermi per negligente,
esendo tropo grand[i] gli oblighi miei di inuigilare sempre al suo seruitio, come farò con il fauore del sig. Dio tuto
il tempo dela mia uita. […] saprà che, oltre quello che di tempo in tempo ho scrito di hauere fato in questo proposito,
ho anco operato dauantagio asai, et per non stancare V. S. Ill.ma con tropo longa scritura ho lasato di scriuere; ma in
efeto pare a me che loro non douriano ricusare il partito che S. M.tà li propone, come io ho scrito al duca di
Epernone, che è di lasare il goue[r]no dela Prouenza [et] quello dela […]

# R22 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 7 October 1588: the Council of Trent, the faculties, Soissons' absolution, Avignon, Épernon)

Translation of `R22_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 132r] This […] to the sheet of cipher that came in Your Most Illustrious Lordship's letters of the 19th of last
month […] there is no need to say, that as to the publication of the Council of Trent I have never failed to do every
most effective office so that it be published freely and without any condition, as I have also reported to Your Most
Illustrious Lordship in several of my letters; and I have already had the promise of all three Estates, though
separately from one another, that all together they will ask for it in their articles (cahiers) to His Majesty. I
shall not fail to continue, using those persuasions that are set out in the said cipher. As to presenting the
faculties of the legation to the Parlement, I already wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with mine of the 12th of
last month that I had presented them […], so advised by persons of the first rank and most devoted to Our Lord and to
that Holy See. His Majesty nevertheless keeps them by him, not having had time to see and consider them; I shall not
fail to do whatever office […] commits to me. But it must be known that if the […] faculties are not verified
(registered) by the Parlement, all the acts I made would be [f. 132v] without life […], since the Parlement is what
has to have them executed and obeyed, as also happens with all the edicts and ordinances the King himself makes: if
they are not verified by the Parlement they are not obeyed, such being the form of government of this kingdom.

As to the absolution of the princes of Vendôme: having seen what Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes me outside the
cipher in several letters, that I must in any case [wait for] further orders before coming to that absolution, and
having then considered what the cipher contains, I have not known what course to take; for though you tell me that you
are sending me the faculty and the manner of absolving them, and that I, as I think fit, may carry it out or delay it
as I judge good for the kingdom, and although I thought I could now give the absolution by virtue of this order, I did
not think I could alter the form that you send me. Since the Count of Soissons would in no way accept it, saying that
he should not be accused [f. 133r] of a sin he had not even thought of, let alone committed, I resolved to defer it,
though with the greatest resentment both of the said Count and of all his people and of the King himself; but, loving
rather to obey precisely the orders of Our Lord than to satisfy others, I believed I could not go further with their
complaint. […] that, having made known to them […], as Your Most Illustrious Lordship wrote me with yours of 22 August,
and I with mine of the 2nd of last month informed Your Most Illustrious Lordship that I had communicated this […] to
Their Majesties and to the Most Illustrious (Cardinals) of Bourbon and of Vendôme, on which they had treated with me of
the form of the absolution, and made the said Count condescend to be content to abjure in the form Your Most
Illustrious Lordship will see in the copy I send you, in which the truth of the fact is told and the substance of it
set down; and it seemed to me that it mattered more to remove those words [f. 133v] that offended these lords. And on
the very day your letters reached me I was to give him the absolution, it having been arranged that the Count,
arriving shortly […] go elsewhere, should alight at the house of my lodging, where the office would have been done
with the due circumstances. But having left his house and come within two leagues of here, it seemed to him he was
receiving a great affront if I did not absolve him. I excused myself by saying […] that I could do no more than I am
[ordered], and that Our Lord [loves] the Count of Soissons and will in any case give him the said absolution, but that,
His Excellency having sent a gentleman to Our Lord for this purpose, […] will send whatever order he sees fit. This
being heard, the Cardinals of Bourbon and of Vendôme came at once to find me, pressing me hard to oblige them with the
absolution; and I, after seeing that they were not [f. 134r] content with the form sent by Your Most Illustrious
Lordship, answered their Most Illustrious Lordships in conformity with what I had said before; whereupon they resolved
to go to the King, with whom they have made a most vigorous office that His Majesty should send […] post-haste to Rome
on this account. And now they come to tell me that the courier leaves within two hours; so I write this in great
haste, but I will not omit to tell you that here they show they know that this change [proceeds] from bad offices done
with Our Lord at the instance of the Cardinal of Sens, by the Most Illustrious Alessandrino, and they complain of [me],
that I exhorted them to send a man express to Our Lord, since many bishops in France had authority to absolve them
without going to Rome. I, from what I know and am informed, find that the Count of Soissons is not more than 20 years
old, and that when he was given to the Cardinal of Bourbon he was not more than 4, and since then he has been brought
up by His Most Illustrious Lordship and has always lived a Catholic, and now he shows himself [f. 134v] most attached
to the Catholic religion; and I fear that making difficulties over the absolution can help neither the Catholic
religion nor the kingdom, because it will certainly make harder the return of Navarre to the obedience of the
Apostolic See, and will be cause of renewing the hatred between this King and those of Guise, since they hold for
certain that all the evil comes from them, though at present, through offices done by me too, they show themselves
quite well disposed together. It seems too that the King resented it much, and wants to put off the opening of the
Estates until the return of this […]; but [with] me His Majesty has not yet spoken of it, as I have not been able to go
and find him, having hurt a foot, which does not let me walk. I hope in one or two days to be able to go out, which I
greatly desire, to make certain whether it is true that the ambassador of the King of Denmark, who I write outside the
cipher has come to this court, comes to persuade His Majesty to unite with his King in defence of the Queen of
England, so as to do in [f. 135r] that case the office that befits the honour of the Lord God and the service of Our
Lord.

I have been much surprised that Monsignor the vice-legate of Avignon complains, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship
writes me in the said cipher, that, though he wrote to me several times on matters important to his government, I
have not answered him; which, were it true, Your Most Illustrious Lordship could with great reason say that this does
not please Our Lord. But you may rest assured that I have had from the said Monsignor […] only three letters on some
business, to all of which I have not only answered by letter but also with all the effects that could come from me, as
Fioravanti his secretary knows very well, who for many months now has stayed at court handling the vice-legate's
business without communicating with me anything but what suits him. The same I can say on the last head of the said
cipher, where you tell me that the Duke of Épernon and La Valette his brother complain of being abandoned by that Holy
See, and that Our Lord wonders that I have not done [f. 135v] the proper office for these lords, as I have been
written by familiar letters, by briefs and by instructions; and I take comfort that Your Most Illustrious Lordship, in
your third letter of the same date of the 19th of last month, outside the cipher, writes me that the office done by
[…] with the Duke of Guise for the benefit of Épernon and his brother, and the letters written to them, have pleased
Our Lord, and that he wills that this business go forward. I therefore pray Your Most Illustrious Lordship to assure
Our Lord that I shall never fail to obey with all promptness the orders of Our Lord, nor do I fear that he will ever
have cause to hold me negligent, my obligations being too great not to watch always over his service, as I shall do
with the favour of the Lord God all the time of my life. […] will know that, besides what I have written from time to
time of having done in this matter, I have also worked a great deal more, and so as not to tire Your Most Illustrious
Lordship with too long a letter I have left off writing it; but in effect it seems to me that they ought not to refuse
the arrangement His Majesty proposes to them, as I have written to the Duke of Épernon, which is to leave the
government of Provence [and] that of the […]

R27, Francia 22/6, n.d. (fragment)

On governments for Épernon (Saintonge, Angoulême, Cognac) and on Boulogne. Épernon's side refuses to give anything back and is said to deal with the Queen of England and Navarre. Morosini hopes for peace between Guise and the others, though with little confidence.

# R27 — Morosini to Montalto, n.d. [Blois, October 1588] (fragment): Épernon's governments and Guise (Francia 22/6, ff. 137r–v)

Rests on: the figures, checked line by line on the DECODE images. DECODE's transcription (HeHan, April 2016) marks many
figures "?"; every line of 137r–v was compared with crops of the image (scratchpad), and the figures read there
(`R27_corrections.tsv`). Segmented first by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R27_worddecode.txt`), then
re-parsed by hand. The leaf is a fragment: 137r begins inside a word ("[m]archesato"); 137v ends after four lines with a
flourish. The "cleartext" images DECODE attached (D1018–D1020) are a clear letter and address leaves, not a
decipherment. Date: after the Duke of Savoy's seizure of the marquisate of Saluzzo (autumn 1588), so Blois, October
1588.
Spelling as the figures give it; punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà, 119
Regina d'Inghilterra, 129 duca di, 132 principe, 144 pace, 151 Francia, 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo, 232 il già Re
di Nauarra). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 137r] [m]archesato di Saluzo, et quello di Angolem[me], di Xantonge et di Cognach, con uno oficio per [?]uno dela
corona, con che posono [?uiuere] con gran dignità, non ci esendo principe in Francia che habia tanti gouerni come loro;
et restituire a S. M.tà Metz et Bologna, perché li a nela conclusione dela pace con questi signori di Guisa
così promeso loro di douer fare. Et nondimeno si mostrano risolutisimi di non uolere restituire alcuna cosa; anzi, per
quello che mi ha deto S. M.tà, tengono pratiche molto [?serate] con la Regina d'Inghilterra, con il già Re di Nauarra,
con Casimiro et con Momoransi; di che mi raferma la sodeta M.tà hauerne certisime proue, onde […] senza gran sospeto di
loro, oltre che, se ei uolese contentare di lasarli tuto, si meteria a mali termini con questi altri. Io non manco
certo, né mancarò per quanto sarà in me, di metere ogni bene, ma spero poco di potere meter pace fra il duca di Guisa et
questi altri, perché al Guisa non mete conto hauere la loro amicitia, poi [?che] l'esere loro innimico è stata la
principale causa di farli guadagnare la afetione et il seguito dei popoli, come per contrario l'h[f. 137v]auere
uoluto il Re sostenerli et fauorir[?li] è stato causa dela sua rouina et d[i] tuti li mali che sono seguiti […].

## Notes on the figures

- "per [?]uno" (137r l. 2): 64 + 17 3 01 191 = "per iuno"; "per ciascuno" would need 25 21 34 ...; left marked.
- "[?uiuere]" (137r l. 3): 3 1 7 3 7 [blot] 0 5 — the ink blot covers two figures; "uiuere" fits what is visible.
- "li a" (137r l. 6): 5 0 1 7 2 1 2: li a, without h (r2p: filled, every figure carries it).
- "[?serate]" (137r l. 10): 4 3 5 0 0 3 5 2 1 5 1 5 3 = s e r e a t e; one e too many for "serrate".
- "onde […]" (137r l. 13): 3 7 1 7 0 3 7 2 9 1 8 4 2 5 2 1 0 0 5 (as on the image) does not parse; "-care/-scare" ending.
- "poi [?che]" (137r l. 20): 7 0 9 1 1 7 1 6 5 0 ...: poi + 1 6 (et?); "che" not carried.
- 137v l. 3 end: "8 4 2 2 7 1 9 5 4 0 1 1 1^. 0 2 3 9 / 2 7 4 2 5 5 6 9 1 6^. 6" does not parse ("... uolta con et questo"?).

# R27 — English (Morosini to Montalto, n.d. [Blois, October 1588], fragment: Épernon's governments and Guise)

Translation of `R27_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 137r] [the m]arquisate of Saluzzo, and that of Angoulême, of Saintonge and of Cognac, with an office of the crown
for each, with which they can [live] in great dignity, there being no prince in France who has so many governments as
they; and to restore Metz and Boulogne to His Majesty, because in concluding the peace with these lords of Guise he
had thus promised them to do. And nevertheless they show themselves most resolved not to restore anything; on the
contrary, from what His Majesty has told me, they are in very [close] dealings with the Queen of England, with the
former King of Navarre, with Casimir and with Montmorency, of which the said Majesty assures me he has most certain
proofs, so that […] without great suspicion of them; besides which, if he were content to leave them everything, he
would put himself on bad terms with these others. I certainly do not fail, nor shall I fail as far as lies in me, to
promote every good, but I have little hope of being able to make peace between the Duke of Guise and these others,
because it does not suit Guise to have their friendship, since being their enemy has been the chief cause of winning
him the affection and the following of the people; just as, on the contrary, the King's having [f. 137v] chosen to
support and favour [them] has been the cause of his ruin and of all the evils that have followed […].

R28, Francia 22/7, [early] Oct [1588] (duplicate)

While walking in the palace garden with the King, the Queen Mother and the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme, Morosini learned that the King would send Signor Girolamo Gondi to Rome about pulling Marshal Montmorency away from the Huguenots. Morosini urged the King to win Guise over with money, since Guise is heavily in debt; Guise refused the grant offered. Vendôme reports that Cardinal Joyeuse worked against the Count of Soissons in Rome.

# R28 — Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [8 October 1588]: the garden talk with Henri III on Montmorency and Guise (Francia 22/7, ff. 142r–145r)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1692 (KaJo, April 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R28_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops; `R28_corrections.tsv`).
The cipher sheet is undated; the clear covering letter on the DECODE "cleartext" image (f. 141) says "Seguiranno queste
poche parole per far coperta all'occlusa cifra ... Di Bles a li viij Ottobre M.D.LXXXVIII", and DECODE's header reads the
sheet as "dup.ta di li viij Otto.", so the date is 8 October 1588 (the sheet is a duplicate). No contemporary
decipherment on the images. Tempesti, *Vita di Sisto V* (1754) II, book VII §§ X–XII, paraphrases this letter closely
(Girolamo Gondi sent to Rome for Montmorency; the garden; "non sarebbe sicura in Bles"; the debts; "per mezzo del Do";
"un donativo di dugentomila scudi"; Guise's refusal); used to recognise names and sense only, never as a source of words.
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes
expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 116 Regina Madre, 129 duca di, 131 cardinale/i, 146 danari, 161 quanto,
165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 226 catolici, 229 ugonotti, 232 il già re di Nauarra).
Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 142r] […] prima che io mi facese […] piede, mi ritrouai una matina a pasegiare in un uiale di questo giardino di
S. M.tà, come soglio fare spese uolte, doue esendo sopra uenuta la Regina Madre, mi posi a pasegiare et ragionar seco;
ma soprauenendo poco dopo S. M.tà, acompagnato da li sig.[ri] cardinali di Borbone e di Uandomo, [?di] Gondi et molta
nobiltà, io mi ritirai con li sodeti sig.[ri] cardinali, lasando che il Re parlase con la regina sua madre. Ma subito mi
chiamarono, et mi presero in mezo fra loro dui, et pasegiando di quel modo incominciò il Re a dirmi che io più uolte,
anco per nome di N. S., l'haueuo esortato a uedere di ritirare a sé il marsciale di Momoransi, et che lui in ciò
conosceua la buona uolontà di N. S. uerso di lui, et però era risoluto di mandarle un gentilomo, che dise che saria il
sig. Hieronimo Gondi, per apresentare a N. S. tuto quello ch'ella pensa di uoler fare a beneficio però [?et] di
[?sodi]sfatione di eso Momoransi, a fine di [ri]tirarlo da l'amicitia del già re di Nauarra et altri heretici et
ridurlo al suo seruitio; et perché conoscendo N. S. [f. 142v] non solo ragioneuoli ma anco importanti tute le sicurtà
che pensa di dare al sodeto Momoransi, [?…] posi ela con l'autorità sua interponersi per condure a buon fine questo
negotio, che desiderauano d'intendere il mio parere; ma che sopra tuto […] uenise secretisimo, perché quando si
risapese non [?mancariano] molti che procurariano disturbare questa riconciliatione. Io le disi che, quanto ala
secreteza, io non ne parlarei con alcuno; ma che 'l dire l'opinione mia sopra questo particolare mi pare superfluo,
poiché molte uolte et con uiue ragioni haueuo esortata S. M.tà a fare ogni opera per ritirare dal'amicitia de li
ugonotti quel signore, et che io teneuo per certo che N. S., che non ha altro fine che il bene uniuersale dela
christianità et l'unione de' catolici ala distrutione del'heresie, non potria hauere nuoua che gli fose più cara che
intendere in questo fato la buona uolontà di S. M.tà, et che io credeuo che non lasaria d'interponere de l'autorità
sua per ridurla a quel fine che si desidera, lodando [f. 143r] asai la persona che S. M.tà pensa di mandare a Roma,
perché è ueram[ente] molto degna per qualsiuoglia carica, et molto diuota et benemerita di cotesta Santa Sede,
hauendo in ogni tempo seruito [?con] tuto il cuore tuti li legati, nuntii et altri che sono mandati dala Sede
Apostolica a questa corte.

Dapoi entrati a parlare di mons. di Guisa, feci eficacisimo oficio per persuadere S. M.tà di pigliar seco confidenza
et leuargli ogni ocasione di sospetione che ela non habi[a] qualche mal animo uerso di lui, perché altram[ente] io
pre[ue]deuo ritornare le cose in pesimi termini; et le considerai che se mons. di Guisa, senza fare altro male, una
matina si partise di corte con quelli dela sua fatione, che moto saria di nuouo in tuto questo regno, et che lei non
si [?stimaria] sicura in Bles, et che partendo non si poteua asicurare di ritirarsi in alcun luogo doue fose riceuta
uolontieri, non temino più mons. di Guisa che S. M.tà, ma temano più loro stesi che gli altri; et sano molto [f. 143v]
bene et in tempo di guerra quando si conuiene hauere apreso soldati et guardie, che [?tanto] male riceuono da gli uni
come da gli altri. Mi dise S. M.tà che quello che le diceuo era uerisimo, et che quanto a lei cercaua di dare ogni
sodisfatione a mons. di Guisa, et di asicurarlo per ogni uia dela sua buona uolontà, et che non sapria fare
d'auantagio, che uole ricordarsi qualche cosa che lo faria […]. Disi che S. M.tà non haueua bisogno di mio
ricordo, ma che tutauia non lasarei di dirle che per opinione mia crederei che due cose giouasero asai per asicurare il
sodeto di Guisa dela buona uolontà dela S. M.tà: la prima era che S. M.tà hauese in efeto nel suo cuore questa buona
uolontà, et l'altra che procurase di mostrarla anco con gli efeti; che mons. di Guisa era carico di debiti et tutauia
continouaua a spendere più che non ha d'entrata, et che S. M.tà, che era liberalisima con gli altri, usase anco con lui
di questa liberalità, perché io mi persuadeuo che li danari sariano benisimo impiegati, et si [?…]riano [f. 144r]
certo il sodeto di Guisa dela buona uolontà di S. M.tà, così rimediando al suo bisogno, non gli permeteriano di pensare
ad altri modi per prouedere ale su[e] necesità. Il Re mi ringratiò molto di questo ricordo, et mi dise che lo uoleua
fare in ogni modo, ma che gli doleua di non hauere al presente comodità di poterlo fare con efeti, poiché non poteua
esere in magior streteza di danari di quello che al presente si ritroua; ma che egli […] daria de le intentione che se
ne saria potuto asicurare. Et io dopo ho inteso che S. M.tà il medesmo giorno gli mandò per mons. d'O a dire che gli
uoleua asignare sopra l'entrate del ano futuro un donatiu[o] di 200 milia scudi, […] non l'ha uoluto acetare,
dicendo che hora la S. M.tà haueua tropo bisogno di danari, et però si riseruaua di acetare di simili fauori quando le
cose fosero in migliore termine. Con tuto ciò pare che dapoi habia […] tratato con S. M.tà molto più apertam[ente] et
con molta [f. 144v] sodisfatione di ambe le parti. Ma l'inimico del'humana natura uole che così apreso S. M.tà come
apreso il duca di Guisa ci siano persone che ad altro non atendono che a nodrire le difidentie et [?seminare]
discordie. Io non manco con tute [?le] parti di fare tuto quello che io poso per fare […] la buona [?intelligenza], [da
la quale] si può sperare la quiete di questo regno et l'istirpatione dele heresie; et per questo fine crederei che fose
molto a proposito che N. S. si contentase di concedere l'asolutione al conte di Suisone nela forma che egli già si è
contentato di fare, rimetendomi però ala singolar prudenza di N. S. et di V. S. Ill.ma.

Hora mi uiene deto dal sig. cardinale Gondi che l'ilustris[simo] di Uandomo le ha deto hauere inteso che il sig.
cardinale di Gioiosa, et non quello di Sans, era stato autore dei mali ofici fati con N. S. contro il conte di Suisons
suo fratelo, et che nel concistoro ala sedia del N. S. haueuano parlato contra li sig.[ri] cardinali Alesandrino et Santi
[f. 145r] Quatro, ma che il medesmo di Gioiosa era stato ale stanze di N. S. a fare il medesmo; che seruirà per auis[o]
a V. S. Ill.ma. […]

## Notes on the figures

- Opening (142r l. 2): "1 1 1 2 2 7 9 6 5 5 4 4 9 0 8" before "prima che" does not parse (the image shows a few more
  figures in the margin, "1 0 1 0 1 2 X", not transcribed); "1 7 1 3 0 2 1 5 0 5 2 5 0" after "facese" gives no word
  ("in alcun" needs 17 0 21 50 25 37 0). The sheet is a duplicate and begins mid-thought.
- "[?di] Gondi" (142r l. 8): 8 26 + 40 91 01 26 17; Tempesti names Gondi among the King's company.
- "[?sodi]sfatione" (142r l. 21): 5 2 21 51 17 91 01 5; 52 (c) read as 57 (sf), a 2/7 slip; the figures for "sodi"
  are not there. Tempesti: "quelle soddisfazioni ch'era disposto di dare al Maresciallo".
- "[ri]tirarlo" (142r l. 22): 1 5 1 7 5 1 1 7 0 0 ...: one figure off.
- "del già re di Nauarra" (142r l. 23): 26 35 05 + 232 (undotted) + 69 et + 2 27 00 171 altri.
- 142v l. 3: "4 5 0 1? 8^.? 7 0 9 1 4 5 1 7 1" after Momoran: the transcriber's "8^.?" is not a code; read
  "[?…] posi" (could be "acciò possa"); left open.
- "desiderauano" (142v l. 5): the figures give desiderauano (21 01 9), kept as written though the subject is the King (r2p).
- "tuto […]" (142v l. 6–7): "6 3 7 = | 1 5 1 9 1" (= is the encipherer's hyphen: tuto) then "1 6 6 4 1 7 1 6" (et per i et?) does not parse.
- "[?mancariano]" (142v l. 8): 20 21 01 25 2 6? 00 21 91 9: one figure uncertain.
- "che [?tanto]" (143v l. 2): 56 21 01 51 9, the t missing.
- "lo faria […]" (143v l. 9): 2 6 1 5 0 9 1 0 1 5 1 1 7 3 5 0 0 3 8? 5 0 1 5 3 does not parse.
- "si [?…]riano" (143v l. 23 – 144r l. 1): 25 91 0 25 13 5 01 62 35 00 17 21 01 9 = "con c r e n d e r i a n o";
  sense "they would assure Guise"; not a word as it stands.
- "egli […] daria" (144r l. 11): 1 0 1 3 9 does not parse.
- "200 milia scudi" (144r l. 16–17): the number is written in plain figures between two null 8s ("8 2 0 0 8"),
  then 20 17 50 17 2 milia; Tempesti: "dugentomila scudi".
- "[…] non l'ha uoluto" (144r l. 17): 1 6 9 5 6 1 2 9 does not parse.
- "habia […] tratato" (144r l. 22): 7 8 4 8 5 2 5 8: nulls and a stray "s e c"; left open.
- 144v ll. 7–9: the paper is damaged (DECODE's comment); "[?seminare]", "per fare […] la buona [?intelligenza]" rest
  on a few legible figures; the image is no better.
- The closing figures (145r ll. 3–4: 8 4 2 2 7 111 2 2 7 9 1 5 4 9 6 0 166 0 1 2 …) were transcribed only in part
  (the transcription line breaks off in corrupt characters); left open.

# R28 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [8 October 1588]: the garden talk with Henri III on Montmorency and Guise)

Translation of `R28_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 142r] […] before I made myself […], I found myself one morning walking in an avenue of this garden of His Majesty,
as I often do, where the Queen Mother having come upon me, I started to walk and talk with her; but His Majesty coming
up shortly after, accompanied by the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme, [?by] Gondi and much nobility, I withdrew with
the said cardinals, leaving the King to talk with the Queen his mother. But they called me at once and took me between
the two of them, and walking in that way the King began to tell me that I had several times, also in the name of His
Holiness, urged him to try to draw Marshal Montmorency to himself, and that in this he recognised the good will of His
Holiness towards him; and therefore he had resolved to send him a gentleman — he said it would be Signor Girolamo
Gondi — to set before His Holiness everything he intends to do for the benefit [and] [?satis]faction of the said
Montmorency, in order to [with]draw him from the friendship of the former King of Navarre and the other heretics and
bring him into his service; and because, His Holiness recognising [f. 142v] not only as reasonable but also as
important all the securities he intends to give the said Montmorency, [?…] she might with her authority interpose
herself to bring this business to a good end, he wished to hear my opinion; but that above all […] it should remain
most secret, because if it became known [?there would not be lacking] many who would try to disturb this
reconciliation. I told him that, as to secrecy, I would not speak of it to anyone; but that to give my opinion on this
particular seemed superfluous to me, since many times and with lively reasons I had urged His Majesty to do everything
to draw that lord away from the friendship of the Huguenots, and that I held it for certain that His Holiness, who has
no other aim than the universal good of Christendom and the union of the Catholics for the destruction of heresy, could
have no news dearer to him than to learn His Majesty's good will in this matter, and that I believed he would not fail
to interpose his authority to bring it to the desired end; praising [f. 143r] highly the person whom His Majesty
intends to send to Rome, because he is truly most worthy of any office, and very devoted to and deserving of that Holy
See, having at all times served [?with] all his heart all the legates, nuncios and others sent by the Apostolic See to
this court.

Then, having come to speak of Monsieur de Guise, I made a most earnest representation to persuade His Majesty to take
him into his confidence and remove from him every cause of suspicion that she [His Majesty] might bear him some ill
will, because otherwise I foresaw matters returning to the worst condition; and I put it to him that if Monsieur de
Guise, without doing any other harm, left the court one morning with those of his faction, there would be a rising
again throughout this kingdom, and that she [His Majesty] would not [?consider herself] safe in Blois, and that, leaving,
she could not be sure of withdrawing to any place where she would be willingly received; [?they do not] fear Monsieur
de Guise more than His Majesty, but fear more for themselves than for the others; and they know very [f. 143v] well,
and in time of war, when one must have soldiers and guards about, that they suffer [?as much] harm from the one side as
from the other. His Majesty told me that what I said was very true, and that for her part she was trying to give every
satisfaction to Monsieur de Guise and to assure him in every way of her good will, and that she could do no more, that
she wanted to be reminded of anything that would make him […]. I said that His Majesty had no need of my reminder, but
that I would nevertheless not fail to tell her that in my opinion two things would greatly help to assure the said
Guise of His Majesty's good will: the first was that His Majesty should truly have this good will in his heart, and the
other that he should take care to show it also by deeds; that Monsieur de Guise was loaded with debts and yet went on
spending more than his income, and that His Majesty, who was most liberal with others, should use this liberality with
him too, because I was persuaded that the money would be very well spent, and [it would assure] [f. 144r] the said
Guise of His Majesty's good will; and so, remedying his need, they would not allow him to think of other ways of
providing for his necessities. The King thanked me much for this advice, and told me that he wanted to do it by all
means, but that he was sorry not to have at present the means to do it in deeds, since he could not be in greater
straits for money than he presently is; but that he […] would give him such intentions as he could be assured of. And I
have since learned that His Majesty on the same day sent Monsieur d'O to tell him that he wished to assign him, on next
year's revenues, a gift of 200,000 scudi; […] he would not accept it, saying that His Majesty now had too much need of
money, and therefore he reserved himself to accept such favours when matters were in a better condition. All the same,
it seems that since then he has […] dealt with His Majesty much more openly and with much [f. 144v] satisfaction on both
sides. But the enemy of human nature wills that, both about His Majesty and about the Duke of Guise, there are persons
who attend to nothing else than feeding mistrust and [?sowing] discord. I do not fail on every side to do all I can to
bring about […] the good [?understanding], [from which] one can hope for the quiet of this kingdom and the rooting out
of heresy; and to this end I would think it very much to the purpose that His Holiness should be content to grant the
absolution to the Count of Soissons in the form in which he has already been content to do it, deferring however to the
singular prudence of His Holiness and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

Now I am told by the Lord Cardinal Gondi that the most illustrious [Cardinal] of Vendôme has told him he has heard that
the Lord Cardinal of Joyeuse, and not the one of Sens, was the author of the bad offices done with His Holiness against
the Count of Soissons his brother, and that in the consistory, at His Holiness's chair, they had spoken against the
Lord Cardinals Alessandrino and Santi [f. 145r] Quattro, but that the same Joyeuse had been in His Holiness's rooms to
do the same; which will serve as a notice to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. […]

R29, Francia 22/8, 10 Oct [1588] (duplicate)

A messenger is back from Florence about the Grand Duke's marriage to the Princess of Lorraine; Orazio Rucellai will conclude it, and the Queen Mother plans to escort her to Marseille. News that the Duke of Savoy has seized the whole marquisate of Saluzzo; Guise fears this will force peace with Navarre and the heretics. Morosini asks for orders; a Danish ambassador is dealing over merchants' goods.

# R29 — Morosini to Montalto, [Blois], 10 October 1588: the Tuscan marriage, Savoy's seizure of Saluzzo, Soissons, Denmark (Francia 22/8, ff. 152r–153v)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1693 (KaJo, April 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R29_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops; `R29_corrections.tsv`).
Date from the docket on 152r, "dup.to di l[ette]ra x Ott." (duplicate of the letter of 10 October; 1588 from the
content: the Duke of Savoy's seizure of Saluzzo, late September–early October 1588); the court and the legate were
at Blois for the Estates. No contemporary decipherment on the DECODE images: the "cleartext" images are Morosini's
letters in clear (address leaf and despatches), not a decipherment of this sheet.
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes
expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 116 Regina Madre, 119 Regina d'Inghilterra, 126 Gran Duca, 129 duca (di),
131 cardinale di, 143 guerra, 144 pace, 152 Franzesi, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma,
213 ambasciatore, 216 auiso, 217 corriere, 226 catolica, 227 heretici, 232 il già re di Nauarra).
Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [word] supplied.

## Reading

[f. 152r] […] hieri sera giunse qui un corriere di ritorno da Firenze, mandato dala Regina Madre per la conclusione del
matrimonio del Gran Duca con questa principesa di Lorena, et riporta che il sig. Horatio Rucelai fra quatro giorni
sarà qui per dare compimento a questo negotio, desiderando il Gran Duca che la sposa per tuto il mese di
[?Nouembre] si ritroui a Marsiglia, doue la Regina Madre medesma pensa di acompagnarla. Questo corriere dice di eser
stato ritenuto quatro giorni in Sauoia, non hauendo quel sig. duca uoluto lasarlo pasare, perché portase nuoua del
impresa fata da S. Alt., la quale, dice eso corriere, che s'è impadronita di tute l[e] piaze del marchesato di Saluzo. Per
il quale auiso sono rimasti qui tuti atoniti, et il sig. duca di Guisa mi ha mandato a dire che uede molto bene che
questo acidente sarà la rouina dela religione catolica, […] a fine di potere far la guerra al duca di Sauoia
procurarano di fare la pace con il già re di Nauarra et con li heretici, non si potendo in un tempo medesmo fare
guerra con gli uni [f. 152v] et con l'altro; et se bene mi promete lui di tenire saldo con tuti li suoi amici
perché non si permeti nel regno altra religione, […] et che inanzi che seguise questo acidente staua sicuro che li Stati
tuti hauriano dimandata la totale distrutione deli altri, che hora temeua che la necesità non li conducese a qualche
altra risolutione. Questo acidente importantisimo et pericolosi, che potria causare grandisimi inconuenienti, mi ha
fato agiungere anco questo al longo dispacio fato hieri, non esendo ancora partito il corriere, desiderando io che
piacia a V. S. Ill.ma darmi ordine di quello che dourò fare quando si uenise a dimandare questa pace uniuersale con
permisione di altra religione che dela catolica, per atendere ala ricuperatione del sodeto marchesato, come si ha
grande da temere, che saria ueram[ente] la totale rouina di questo regno et dela religione.

Per rimediare ale male contenteze del Re et di questo sig. di Borbone per la negatiua [f. 153r] del'asolutione del
conte di Suisons, et credendo che si[?a] seruitio di N. S. radolcirli, per leuare anco l'ocasioni di magiore
[?romori], ho procurato con il mezo del sig. cardinale di Gondi di persuadere che uoglino contentarsi di fare
l'abiuratione nel modo et forma mandatami da V. S. Ill.ma; il che è causa che si tratiene il corriere, per uedere di
ridurli a questo; né ancora ho hauto risolutione di quello che intendono di fare.

Hor hora mi uiene deto che qui si laudano grandem[ente] de i buoni ofici fati dal nuntio di N. S. residente in Turino
in questa ocasione dela presa dele […] sodete piaze con quel duca.

Il sig. cardinale di Gondi mi ha asicurato che l'ambasciatore di Danimarcha non ha tratato qui altro negotio che la
restitutione di alcune mercantie leuate a' suditi del suo Re da uaseli franzesi, et che non è uero che habi parlato per
la Regina d'Inghilterra né d'altro particolare. Il medesmo ho anco [?inteso] per altra uia: egli non ha parlato più
[f. 153v] che una uolta con il Re, et poche […] parole, et hora solecita [?con] molta diligenza sua speditione, la
quale S. M.tà ha [?comandato] che si facia […].

## Notes on the figures

- 152r l. 2: the opening "5 5 4 7 2 2 1 2 1 6 9 5 2 1 2 1 8" (con, st, a …) does not parse.
- "corriere" (152r l. 2): the encipherer wrote "2 1 2" with the dot, and a 7 above the last figure: 212 corrected to 217
  (corriere) on the page. 152r l. 11 "questo corriere": 166, then "1 2 1 7" (a stray 1 before 217 without its dot).
- "dala Regina Madre per" (152r l. 3): "1 1 6^. 6 4" = 116 + 64 (decoder: 166).
- "del Gran Duca con questa principesa" (152r l. 4): "1 2 6 1 9 1 6^. 6" = 126 without its dot, 19 con, 166 with the
  dot on the 6.
- "qui" (152r l. 7): the image has 9 7 (qui); DECODE reads 9 1 (r2p).
- "[?Nouembre]" (152r l. 9): 9 1 9 1 3 7 3 5 0 2 4 2 0 0 3 5 = o o u e m b r e; the first 91 for 01 (n)?
- "medesma pensa" (152r l. 10): "?20." is not a code: 20 35 26 35 45 20 2 (medesma) 70 35 01 45 2 (pensa).
- "quel sig. duca" (152r l. 13): 4 17 40 + 1 2 9 (129 without its dot); likewise "il sig. duca di Guisa" (l. 18).
- "S. Alt." (152r l. 15): 4 37 2 8 2 27 8 (sua + a lt + null; the 8 closes the abbreviation).
- "dice eso corriere" (152r l. 16): 2 1 7 = 217 without its dot.
- 152r l. 21: "1 7 1 0 1 5 1 6 5" before "a fine di" does not parse.
- "l'altro, et se bene" (152v l. 1): 50 2 27 00 9, 1 6 = et.
- 152v l. 4: "5 6 5 0 2 2 2 6" (che, l, a, a, d) before "et che inanzi" does not parse.
- "hora temeua" (152v l. 7): the dot on 1 4^. 9 (149 Italiani) is spurious: 14 91 00 2 = hora.
- "necesità" (152v l. 7): 2 0 for 1 0 (m for n).
- "ueram[ente]" (152v l. 20): 3 35 00 21 20 8, m + 8 the -mente abbreviation.
- "il corriere" (152v l. 14): 2 1 7 without its dot.
- "sig. di Borbone" (152v l. 23): "4 1^. 7 4 0 8" = s i g + 8 (abbreviation), the dot spurious, no code 417.
- "credendo" (153r l. 2): 22 35 3? 6 35 01 26 191; the uncertain 3 must be 2 (26 = d). "si[?a]": 4 1 7 1 7 1.
- "cardinale di Gondi" (153r ll. 4, 15): 1 3 1 (131 without its dot) + 40 91 01 26 17.
- "per uedere" (153r l. 9): 64, 3 3 5 2 6 3 5 0 0 5 (one 3 doubled); "il corriere" before it: 2 1 7 without dot.
- "dele […] sodete piaze" (153r l. 15): "1 1 3" (113 without dot?) after dele does not fit.
- "da uaseli franzesi" (153r l. 19): 3 21 45 35 05 7 + 152.
- 153v l. 1: "4 5 1 7 2 0 5" between poche and parole does not parse; 153v ll. 4–5: "4 2 2 7 9 1 2 1 3^. 0 1 2 7 4 2 9
  6 0 1 0 2" at the end does not parse.

## Translation

[f. 152r] […] yesterday evening a courier arrived here on his way back from Florence, sent by the Queen Mother for the
conclusion of the Grand Duke's marriage with this Princess of Lorraine. He reports that Signor Orazio Rucellai will be
[here] within four days to complete this business, the Grand Duke wishing the bride to be at Marseille by the end of
[November], where the Queen Mother herself intends to accompany her. This courier says he was held for four days in
Savoy, that Lord Duke not having been willing to let him pass, so that he should not carry news of the enterprise
carried out by His Highness, who, the said courier says, has made himself master of all the strongholds of the
marquisate of Saluzzo. At this news everyone here is left astonished, and the Duke of Guise has sent to tell me that he
sees very well that this event will be the ruin of the Catholic religion: […] in order to be able to make war on the
Duke of Savoy they will try to make peace with the former King of Navarre and with the heretics, since one cannot at
the same time make war on the one [f. 152v] and on the other. And although he promises me to hold firm, with all his
friends, so that no other religion is permitted in the kingdom, […] and that before this event happened he was sure that
the Estates would all have demanded the total destruction of the others, whereas now he feared that necessity might
lead them to some other resolution. This most important and dangerous event, which could cause very great
mischief, has made me add this too to the long despatch of yesterday, the courier not having left yet, as I wish Your
Most Illustrious Lordship to be pleased to give me orders on what I am to do if it came to asking for this universal
peace, with permission of a religion other than the Catholic, in order to attend to the recovery of the said
marquisate, as is greatly to be feared; which would truly be the total ruin of this kingdom and of religion.

To remedy the discontents of the King and of this Lord of Bourbon at the refusal [f. 153r] of absolution for the
Count of Soissons, and believing it to be in Our Lord's service to soften them, and also to remove the occasions of
greater [disturbances], I have tried, through the Cardinal de Gondi, to persuade them to be content to make the
abjuration in the manner and form Your Most Illustrious Lordship sent me; and this is why the courier is being held, to
see whether they can be brought to this. I have not yet had their resolution on what they intend to do.

Just now I am told that here they greatly praise the good offices done by Our Lord's nuncio resident in Turin on this
occasion of the taking of the said […] strongholds by that Duke.

The Cardinal de Gondi has assured me that the ambassador of Denmark has treated nothing else here than the restitution
of certain merchandise taken from his King's subjects by French ships, and that it is not true that he spoke for the
Queen of England or on any other particular matter. I have [heard] the same by another way: he has not spoken more
[f. 153v] than once with the King, and few […] words; and he is now pressing [with] great diligence for his
despatch, which His Majesty has [ordered] to be made […].

R30, Francia 22/9, 3 Oct [1588], Blois

Morosini took on the job of reconciling the Duke of Guise and Mons. de Nevers, who have been at odds since they married sisters; with the King's approval, both promised to follow his advice. He pressed Guise and the Cardinal of Guise on publishing the council. The clergy is split: the lower deputies want Gallican liberty reserved.

# R30 — Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 3 October 1588: reconciling Nevers and Guise, the Council of Trent, the clergy and the Gallican liberties (Francia 22/9, ff. 162v, 162r, 161v, 161r, 160r)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1694 (KaJo, May 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R30_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand
on the transcribed figures (`R30_corrections.tsv`). Date and place from the clear docket at the head of 162v as
transcribed by DECODE ("Del s. Car. Mo[rosini] … 3 ottobre da Bles"). No contemporary decipherment on the DECODE
images (the record has no "cleartext" images); Rome's decipherments (Francia 27) are not imaged. Tempesti (1754)
mentions the Nevers–Guise quarrel and the clergy's resistance to the Council only in outline; not used for words.
Page order: the transcription lists the pages in reverse foliation (162v, 162r, 161v, 161r, 160r), and that is the
reading order: the docket heads 162v, and every page turn continues the sentence (162v "a S. M.tà andai …" → 162r "a
ritrouarla"; 162r "si maritò nela" → 161v "sorela dela sua moglie"; 161v "cardinale di Guisa" → 161r "suo fratelo";
161r "ne mancarò" → 160r "di fare ogni oficio"). The leaf is bound reversed. 160r ends in mid-sentence; the rest of the
cipher (160v?) is not among the DECODE images.
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes
expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 129 duca di, 131 cardinale di, 135 uescoui, 141 clero, 165/166 quello/questo
in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma); "sua Ecel." / "S. E." (4 8 153 8) = Sua Eccellenza, Nevers at 162v, Guise at 162r l. 19
(feminine agreement "uenuta", "la quale"; "ritrouarla", "ela", "lei" at 162r ll. 1–9 are S. M.tà); m + 8 = -mente. Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [x] supplied.

## Reading

[f. 162v] Et l'altre […] i ragionamenti hauti con mons. di Niuers ho scoperto asai manifestamente una mala
sodisfatione che sua Ecel. tiene con mons. di Guisa, dela quale se bene anco prima io ne haueuo qualche notitia, non
credeuo però che ela fose giunta a termine di potere aportare quel male ala quiete di questo regno che dipoi ho
conosciuto. Però mi parue di fare con S. E. ogni eficace oficio per meterla d'acordo con il sodeto duca di Guisa,
conoscendo che il continouare loro in mala inteligenza insieme era causa che così l'uno come l'altro non lascia
di fare di mali ofici con il Re, a graue pregiudicio dela quiete et conseruatione dela […]; et dopo molte ragioni et
persuasioni, seruendomi anco dela autorità di […] N. S., con dire che questa unione saria gratisima a N. S., lo ridusi a
termini che, dopo una longa narratiua di ofese che diceua di hauere riceute dal sodeto di Guisa, finalmente si contentò
di prometermi di fare in ciò tuto quello che io giudicasi conueniente. Però, a fine di procedere in questo negotio con
quella circonspetione che conuiene et non dare alcuna sospetione a S. M.tà, andai li giorni […] pasati [f. 162r] a
ritrouarla, et le considerai il dano che ela riceueua da questa disunione, che è grandisimo per ogni rispeto, ma
principalm[ente] perché, per nuocersi l'uno et l'altro, ueniuano anco il più dele uolte a nuocere a le cose del suo
seruitio, oltre ala confusione che nasceua nel animo di S. M.tà per le difidentie et sospeti che erano seminati fra lei
et gli altri; et mi ofersi d'interpormi fra loro per riconciliarli insieme, se la lo trouaua buono, […] disi che non
haueuo uoluto ponere mano se prima non sapeuo la mente di S. M.tà, con tuto che hauesi dal duca di Niuers la parola
che si contentaua di fare tuto quello che io hauesi giudicato conueniente. Mostrò il Re di hauere gratisimo questo
oficio, confesando che saria di gran bene ale cose sue se questi si quietasero insieme, et mi pregò di parlarne con
mons. di Guisa et uedere di ridurlo a questa compositione, come feci il giorno seguente, e[s]endo S. E. uenuta a
uedermi; la quale, se bene uolese […] darmi conto di tute le mali sodisfationi che le haueua date mons. di Niuers,
incominciando per sino dal tempo che si maritò nela [f. 161v] sorela dela sua moglie, tutauia in fine dise che, con
tuto che io [?fidase] molto nela parola che io diceuo esermi stata data dal sodeto duca di Niuers, et ela ancora mi
prometeua di fare tuto quello che a me parese conueniente. Hora si atenderà a formare i capitoli del acordo con il
consenso et uolontà del Re, per uedere di dar fine a così buona et salutare riconciliatione, nela quale non
mancarano molte dificoltà. Piacia al sig. Dio di fauorirmi con la sua santis. gratia, che io, per quello sarà in me,
non lasarò di afaticarmi con tuto lo spirito; et di quello seguirà ne darò auiso a V. S. Ill.ma.

Feci anco con mons. di Guisa eficacisimo uficio per la publicatione del concilio di Trento, dicendoli apertam[ente]
che io sapeuo che fra il sig. cardinale suo fratelo et lui haueuano tanta parte et autorità neli Stati che, quando
unitam[ente] non dimandasero la publicatione di eso concilio, […] saria de loro: non hauriano procurato da uero. Mi
promise il sig. duca […] di fare ogni suo potere, et tuto quel più che io gli hauesi ricordato. Simile oficio ho fato
con il sig. cardinale di Guisa [f. 161r] suo fratelo et con tuti quelli che mi uengono a parlare; ma ho inteso che,
esendo stato proposto l'altra matina fra il clero questo punto, si era scoperta fra di loro una grandisima diuisione,
esendo che, da li uescoui in fuori, tuti gli altri deputati inferiori, non ricusando la publicatione del concilio,
uogliono che prima si uega quello che pregiudica ala libertà dela chiesa galicana, et che questo sii in ogni modo
ecetuato. Non ho mancato anco di parlare a S. M.tà, esortandola a publicare esa di sua spontanea uolontà il sodeto
concilio senza aspetare di esere ricercata dai Stati; et se pretenderà qualche gratia, che già sapeua quello che io
per nome di N. S. le haueuo promeso, che in tute le cose honeste saria compiaciuta; et mi ha promeso di così fare. Io
non mancarò di continouare li ofici con quella magiore instanza che mi sarà posibile, et di quanto seguirà ne
ragua[g]liarò V. S. Ill.ma. Ho [?inteso] hora che una dele cose che si propone fra lo stato eclesiastico si […] che da
N. S. non si posino concedere alienationi di beni eclesiastici in questo regno senza il consenso del clero; et io non
ho mancato, né mancarò, [f. 160r] di fare ogni oficio perché non si uenga a tratare questo punto, con dire che non
aspeta a loro di metere mano nela potestà di N. S., et che era anco superfluo il tratarne, perché io credeuo certo che
N. S., né con il consenso né senza, permeterà più uendita di beni dela chiesa, poi che pur tropo se ne erano uenduti
con molto dispiacere di N. S., che nisuna cosa desidera più che la sua conseruatione et indemnità […] N. S. […] a
questo […]

## Notes on the figures

- Opening (162v l. 2): "69 05 2 27 80 35" = et l'altre (80 for 00), then 171 before "ragionamenti"; the sentence seems
  to continue a sheet not imaged, or "l'altre" refers to earlier letters.
- "con S. E." (162v l. 9, Nevers) and "S. E. uenuta" (162r l. 19, Guise): 4 8 153 8, s and e each closed by the
  abbreviation 8; the feminine agreement is Italian usage with "Eccellenza".
- "eficace oficio" (162v l. 9): figures 153 03 17 25 21 5 25 9 30 17 25 17 9 (c and e transposed).
- "lascia di fare" (162v l. 13): 50 21 34 17 212 | 62 171 = lascia di (r2p; the -ua of lasciaua is not written).
- "dela […]; et dopo" (162v l. 15): 2 1 2 1 4? 2 3 2 1 2 2 2 6 open.
- "di […] N. S." (162v l. 16): 2 6 5 7 1 before 111 open.
- "andai li giorni […] pasati" (162v l. 24): 0 1 7 between giorni and pasati.
- "nuocersi" (162r l. 3): 0 3 2 9 1 2 5 3 5 0 0 4 5 7 (one stray 2); DECODE decode "per nuocere et fnito".
- "[…] disi" (162r l. 10): 1 7 1 0 5 6 before "disi" open.
- "uolese […] darmi conto" (162r l. 20): 5 0 3 5 7 9 open; "darmi" has a doubled 2.
- "[?fidase]" (161v l. 2): figures 30 17 62 45 21 54 5 (f i d s a s e).
- "[…] saria de loro" (161v l. 19): 2 1 2 5 0? 3 5 6 8 open.
- "duca […] di fare" (161v l. 21): DECODE "129. ?26." (an unreadable figure); Guise is meant.
- "si […] che" (161r l. 21): 7 1? after "si" open.
- 160r l. 9 (last line): "8 4 2 5 9 [111] 2 7 0 0 1 3 2 2 [166] 2 0 1 3 7 7 6 9 7 0" does not parse; the sentence runs
  on to a page not imaged.
- Recurring transcription habits: 30 for 70 (p) in "questo punto" (160r l. 2); "pr", "fr" written 7 0 0 0 / 3 0 0 0
  (proposto, propone, pretenderà, fra); 64 = per inside words (scoperto, scoperta, superfluo, apertam.).

# R30 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 3 October 1588: reconciling Nevers and Guise, the Council of Trent, the clergy)

Translation of `R30_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 162v] And the other […] from the conversations I have had with Monsieur de Nevers I have discovered quite plainly
an ill feeling that His Excellency (Nevers) has towards Monsieur de Guise; of which, though I had some notice of it before, I
did not believe it had come to the point of being able to bring the harm to the quiet of this kingdom that I have
since recognised. So it seemed right to me to do every effective office with His Excellency to bring him to agreement
with the said Duke of Guise, knowing that their continuing on bad terms together was the reason why both the one and
the other did not [cease] to do ill offices with the King, to the grave prejudice of the quiet and preservation of the
[…]; and after many reasons and persuasions, using also the authority of […] Our Lord, saying that this union would be
most welcome to Our Lord, I brought him to the point that, after a long account of the offences he said he had
received from the said Guise, he at last agreed to promise me to do in this all that I should judge proper. So, in
order to proceed in this business with the circumspection it requires and to give no suspicion to His Majesty, I went
some days ago [f. 162r] to find His Majesty, and put to him the harm he was suffering from this disunion, which is very great
in every respect, but principally because, in harming each other, the one and the other came most often to harm the
affairs of his service as well, besides the confusion that arose in His Majesty's mind from the distrust and
suspicions sown between him and the others; and I offered to interpose myself between them to reconcile them, if His
Majesty thought it good; […] I said that I had not wished to put my hand to it unless I first knew His Majesty's mind,
although I had the Duke of Nevers' word that he would do all I should judge proper. The King showed that he found this
office most welcome, admitting that it would be of great benefit to his affairs if they made peace together, and he
asked me to speak of it to Monsieur de Guise and see whether I could bring him to this settlement, as I did the next
day, His Excellency (Guise) having come to see me; who, though he wished […] to give me an account of all the grievances
Monsieur de Nevers had given him, beginning from the time he married the [f. 161v] sister of his (Guise's) wife,
nevertheless said in the end that, although I [trusted] much in the word that I said had been given me by the said
Duke of Nevers, he too promised me to do all that I should think proper. Now they will set about drawing up the
articles of the agreement with the King's consent and will, to see whether so good and salutary a reconciliation can
be completed, in which there will be no lack of difficulties. May it please the Lord God to favour me with His most
holy grace, for I, as far as lies in me, shall not fail to labour at it with all my spirit; and of what follows I shall
inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

I also made a most effective office with Monsieur de Guise for the publication of the Council of Trent, telling him
openly that I knew that the Cardinal his brother and he had so much part and authority in the Estates that, if they did
not jointly ask for the publication of the Council, […] would be theirs: they would not have worked for it in earnest.
The Duke […] promised me to do all in his power, and everything more that I should remind him of. I have done a
similar office with the Cardinal of Guise [f. 161r] his brother and with all who come to speak to me; but I have heard
that, this point having been proposed among the clergy the other morning, a very great division had appeared among
them, since, apart from the bishops, all the other lower deputies, while not refusing the publication of the Council,
want it first seen what prejudices the liberty of the Gallican church, and that this be excepted in any case. I have
also not failed to speak to His Majesty, urging him to publish the said Council of his own free will without waiting
to be asked by the Estates; and if he should claim some favour, he already knew what I had promised him in Our Lord's
name, that in all honest things he would be gratified; and he has promised me to do so. I shall not fail to continue
the offices with the greatest insistence I can, and of all that follows I shall inform Your Most Illustrious Lordship.
I have [heard] now that one of the things proposed among the ecclesiastical estate is […] that Our Lord may not grant
alienations of church property in this kingdom without the consent of the clergy; and I have not failed, nor shall I
fail, [f. 160r] to do every office so that this point is not taken up, saying that it does not belong to them to lay
hands on Our Lord's power, and that it was also superfluous to discuss it, because I was sure that Our Lord, neither
with their consent nor without it, will allow any more sale of church property, since all too much has been sold, to
the great displeasure of Our Lord, who desires nothing more than its preservation and indemnity […] Our Lord […] to
this […]

R31, Francia 22/10, 23 Oct [1588], Blois

Mandelot, governor of Lyon, is ordered to arrest a man for transfer to Avignon. The Cardinal of Guise asks for the vice-legation of Avignon. The Florentine marriage contract is going forward.
