# R43 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, 23 December 1588: the killing of the Duke of Guise)

Translation of `R43_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 308r] […] this morning […] the Duke of Guise was killed in the King's chamber, by order of His Majesty, with dagger
blows, and his death came about in this way. His Majesty had been warned from several quarters of the evil intention
that the said Guise had against his person; and Signor Alfonso Corso having arrived here, as Your Most Illustrious
Lordship will have heard by my last letters, sent by the Duke of Mayenne for the reasons written, with warnings that His
Majesty should keep good guard against Monsieur de Guise his brother, who was plotting against his person, and that he
himself would have come to Blois had he thought he could arrive in time to turn him from his designs; and the said Duke
of Guise having told His Majesty yesterday [likewise] that, were the Estates General not sitting, he would with his own
hand have killed many of those who stood around him and always did him bad offices, adding many other threatening words
— for these reasons the King at last, without communicating this thought to any living person, resolved in his mind to
take his life. Yesterday evening he gave out that he would go hunting this morning, and he let some men know (who are
not named so far) that they should be in the cabinet at five in the morning, as they did; and when they had come to His
Majesty he opened his mind to them, and having found them most ready to carry it out, he had them [f. 308v] stay in the
chamber and sent to call the Duke of Guise, who was in the Council of State. He came, and as soon as he entered the
chamber he was seized by two men from the side and thrown down by others with many dagger blows, after making a great
defence in vain with his hands and his teeth, without ever being able to put his hand to his sword. While the deed was
being done His Majesty stayed withdrawn in the cabinet with Signor Alfonso Corso alone, whom he keeps with him as his
guard. Guise dead, and the Cardinal of Guise (who was also in the Council), the Duke of Nemours, the Duke of Elbeuf, the
Prince of Joinville, the Archbishop of Lyon, the prévôt des marchands of Paris and the president de Neuilly made
prisoners, and a guard set on the Cardinal of Bourbon, the King went to find the Queen Mother and told her the reasons
why he had been forced to forestall the Duke's designs, to free himself from danger and the kingdom from tyranny. The
Queen Mother remained astonished and could not answer a word. Until all this had been done the guards stood under arms,
and all the gates and principal […] of the town were taken, in which […] and no disturbance has followed.

As soon as I was told by my household, who from the windows had seen the castle gates being shut and the guards
taking up arms, I tried to learn [f. 309r] the reason, and was told that the King wanted to have a man arrested who had
put his hand to a dagger in His Majesty's chamber; nor could the truth be learned until the Cardinal de Gondi, in His
Majesty's name, came to give me the news of what had happened and the reasons that had forced him to that execution,
both what has been said above, learned through the Duke of Mayenne, and other things written by that d'Aumale, his
first cousin. I did not know what to answer, being left half dead by this news; and yet I told him that I wept for the
misfortune of that prince and prayed God that it might not be to the greater harm and ruin of this kingdom. I tried to
have an audience, but it has not been possible, His Majesty excusing himself with the many business he had. I will not
cease to go on asking for it, to perform at least the office I owe for those who remain alive; and from what the
Cardinal de Gondi tells me, it can be held for certain that they will not die. His Majesty then went to mass and dined
in public without showing any change [in his face?], and the Cardinal de Vendôme gave him the napkin for his hands. A
proclamation has been issued that all the masters of houses must today give in the names of all those lodging with
them; and His Majesty has since let the Dukes of Nemours and Elbeuf know [f. 309v] that they should be of good cheer,
for they will not be harmed. It has [likewise] been […] ordered, on pain of death, that no one may leave Blois without
a written licence. For all that, many servants and friends of the Duke of [Guise] have cleared out. I am assured that His
Excellency was warned yesterday from several quarters to beware of the King, but […] that he could not persuade himself
that His Majesty would take such a resolution — or else his hour had come. […] I have said […]. […] I am assured that the
Cardinal of Guise too is dead, which however I cannot know for certain, though I much fear it, knowing the King's great
displeasure with His Most Illustrious Lordship for the words he spoke freely against his person, and because he knew
that it was he who pushed the Estates against him. I am also told that His Majesty has sent to the Duke of Nevers,
begging him urgently to attend more than ever to the war against Navarre, being quite resolved to continue with all his
power to root out heresy from his kingdom, so that the world should not believe that he has made it rather to please
the Duke of Guise than from his own inclination [f. 307r] [up to now]. His Majesty has also sent Signor Alfonso Corso to
Lyon with letters patent as his lieutenant general of the forces that are with the Duke of Mayenne, and writes to His
Excellency that, [moved] chiefly by the warning that he had sent him through the said Signor Alfonso Corso, in agreement
with many others of the same tenor he had had from several quarters, he had resolved to carry out that execution against
the Duke of Guise, which he would understand, and which he believed […] blame; […] he had been driven to it not by
hatred of his house but by pure necessity of saving his life and quieting his kingdom; and therefore on every occasion
he would show him, in his own person, his wish to help and gratify him; but for the present he urged him to withdraw to
his government and hand over the forces intended for the Dauphiné enterprise to the said Signor Alfonso, because when
[…] he sees him take this deed in the way he should, he will not fail to honour his person with greater favours. I find
myself so troubled and confused, and I shall await with most ardent desire an answer […] with the order that it will
please [f. 307v] Our Lord to give me; and I kiss Your Most Illustrious Lordship's hands again […].

R44, Francia 22/23, dup., 24 Xbre [1588], [Blois]

The Cardinal of Guise was put to death only this morning. Because he was a churchman, Morosini leaves the response to the Pope's judgment. The Cardinal de Bourbon is under guard and ill, and Joinville and the Archbishop of Lyon are to go to Amboise.

# R44 — Morosini to Montalto, [Blois], 24 December 1588 (duplicate): the death of the Cardinal of Guise (Francia 22/23, ff. 313r–314r, 315r)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1709 (KaJo, Jan 2016) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R44_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures and, at the doubtful places, on the DECODE images (crops; `R44_corrections.tsv`). The clear
heading on 313r reads "dup.to 24 X.bre". The letter runs 313r–314r and ends there; 315r is a separate cipher leaf
(postscript or a sheet of another letter) beginning inside a sentence ("[…] lasare di dire"). The "cleartext" images on
DECODE (D1076, D1085) are a clear letter and an address leaf, not a decipherment. Tempesti (1754), book IX, reports the
same events (the Cardinal of Guise killed the day after his brother; the secretary's examination); used for names
only.
Spelling as the figures give it; punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (111 N. S., 113 S. M.tà /
il Re, 116 Regina Madre, 129 duca di, 131 cardinale di, 132 principe di, 133 arciuescouo, 161 quanto, 165/166
quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 215 secretario, 221 lettera, 227 heretici). Marks: [?word] partly
carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 313r] Quando [?io] scrisi hieri sera a V. S. Ill.ma che oltre la morte del sig. duca di Guisa che […] si diceua che
era morto ancora il sig. cardinale suo fratelo, et non fu uero alhora, ma questa matina solam[ente] è rimasto priuo di
uita: alcuni dicono di fero come il fratelo, altri con una fune strangolato, che per ancora non si intende il uero. Mi
uiene deto che il Re si sii risoluto di farlo morire hauendo scoperto che egli disegnaua di fugire, et che per questo
efeto si uedeua qualche soleuatione di gente. Di questa morte io sono rimasto molto più confuso che di quella del sig.
duca di Guisa, esendo persona eclesiastica et cardinale, né so come gouernarmi, temendo di erare in tuti modi. Ma dopo
hauere maturam[ente] considerato tuto quello che può sucedere, ho risoluto, poiché da ciò non segue alcun pregiudicio
ala santità di N. S. né a cotesta santa sede, et può sempre usare la sua autorità, di uolere più tosto andare
destregiando con rimostrare al Re il suo erore et contenerlo nela debita ubidientia ala santa sede apostolica, che esere
io l'autore di qualche scandalosa risolutione, dela quale, per quello che io uego, si può asai temere quando si hauese da
tratare con termini più rigorosi; et in cosa di tanta importanza et consequenza ho stimato più conueniente di lasare il
giuditio ala soma prudentia [f. 313v] di N. S., che uolere deliberare da me. Però la suplico con ogni humiltà a farmi
quanto prima sapere la risoluta uolontà di N. S. Dimani io andarò dal Re, hauendomi hogi mandato S. M.tà un biglieto
scrito di sua mano, la tradutione del quale sarà con questa.

Il sig. cardinale di Borbone sta tutauia guardato dale guardie del Re, se bene nel leto con febre et un [f]luso di sangue,
che, agionta la mala contenteza et il timore che ha, potria facilmente fargli perdere la uita, come […] bene, dicono che
sarà mandato in prigione insieme con il principe di Ianuile nel castelo d'Amboisa, come anco l'arciuescouo [di] Lione, in
qualche altro loco sicuro. Hogi hano esaminato il secretario di mons. di Guisa, hauendogli prima promesa la uita se diceua
il uero di quello che gli sarà dimandato; et fra molte altre cose ha deto che pochi giorni prima N. S. hauea scrito al
sodeto duca una lettera di tre faciate di carta tuta di propria mano in fauore del sig. duca di Sauoia per le cose del
marchesato di Saluzo. Et mi uiene deto che S. M.tà lo raconto ala Regina Madre, dicendole che questi non erano ofici da
padre comune, et che se N. S. uolese procedere seco di questa maniera, che lui ancora faria dal suo canto quello che le
conueniua, non uolendo [f. 314r] […]: "Monsignore legato, hora io sono il Re, et ho preso tal risolutione di non uolere
più soferire ingiurie né mali tratamenti, che io continouarò, a dano di chi si uoglia, la mia generosa risolutione, con
l'esempio del nostro santo padre N. S.", esendomi bene ricordato dela forma del parlare che tiene continouam[ente], che
bisogna farsi obedire et castigare quelli che ci ofendono. Poiché io ho conseguito il fine, [?io] uederò dimani se […]
Dio […].

[f. 315r, a separate leaf] […] lasare di dire a V. S. Ill.ma che S. M.tà per questo auuenimento sucesole così
intieram[ente] a sua sodisfatione, poiché senza mouimento anche minimo o alteratione di popoli è uenuta al disopra di
questi suoi inimici, che da tuto il mondo erano stimati insuperabili, n'ha presa tanta confidenza che con molta facilità,
quando fose astreta, potria mostrarne risentimento […] heretici […].

# R44 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois], 24 December 1588, duplicate: the death of the Cardinal of Guise)

Translation of `R44_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 313r] When [I] wrote to Your Most Illustrious Lordship yesterday evening that, besides the death of the Duke of
Guise, […] it was said that his brother the Cardinal was dead too, it was not true then; but only this morning has he
been deprived of life: some say by the sword like his brother, others strangled with a rope, for the truth is not yet
known. I am told that the King resolved to have him die having discovered that he was planning to flee, and that for
this purpose some rising of people was to be seen. By this death I have been much more confounded than by that of the
Duke of Guise, he being an ecclesiastical person and a cardinal, and I do not know how to conduct myself, fearing to err
in every way. But after maturely considering all that may happen, I have resolved — since no prejudice follows from it
to His Holiness or to that Holy See, and he can always use his authority — to choose rather to proceed with dexterity,
showing the King his error and keeping him in due obedience to the Holy Apostolic See, than to be myself the author of
some scandalous decision, of which, from what I see, there is much to fear if one had to deal in harsher terms; and in a
matter of such importance and consequence I have thought it more fitting to leave the judgement to the supreme wisdom
[f. 313v] of Our Lord than to wish to decide it myself. I therefore beg you with all humility to let me know as soon as
possible Our Lord's settled will. Tomorrow I shall go to the King, His Majesty having today sent me a note written in his
own hand, the translation of which will come with this letter.

The Cardinal de Bourbon is still guarded by the King's guards, although in bed with fever and a flux of blood, which,
added to his discontent and the fear he is in, could easily cost him his life; as […], they say he will be sent to prison
together with the Prince of Joinville in the castle of Amboise, as will the Archbishop of Lyon, to some other safe place.
Today they examined Monsieur de Guise's secretary, having first promised him his life if he told the truth about what he
would be asked; and among many other things he said that a few days before, Our Lord had written to the said Duke a
letter of three sides of paper, all in his own hand, in favour of the Duke of Savoy over the affairs of the marquisate of
Saluzzo. And I am told that His Majesty related this to the Queen Mother, telling her that these were not the offices of
a common father, and that if Our Lord chose to proceed with him in this manner, he too for his part would do what suited
him, not wishing [f. 314r] […]: "Monsignor Legate, now I am King, and I have taken such a resolution not to suffer any
more insults or ill treatment, that I shall carry on my generous resolution, to the harm of whoever it may be, with the
example of our Holy Father, Our Lord" — for I well remember the form of words he constantly uses, that one must make
oneself obeyed and punish those who offend us. Since I have reached the end, [I] shall see tomorrow whether […] God
[…].

[f. 315r, a separate leaf] […] fail to tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship that His Majesty, this event having turned out
so entirely to his satisfaction — since without the least movement or disturbance of the people he has got the upper
hand over these enemies of his, who were reckoned invincible by all the world — has gained such confidence from it that,
were he pressed, he could very easily show resentment […] heretics […].

R45, Francia 22/24, n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589, after Catherine de' Medici's death]

Morosini defends his conduct. The Archbishop of Lyon refuses lay examiners because he is primate of France. The Estates' article excluding Navarre carries a clause reserving the Bourbon succession.

# R45 — Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [mid-]January 1589: audience with Henry III on Navarre, Nevers, the Council of Trent (Francia 22/24, ff. 357r–361v)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1710 (KaJo, Jan 2016) under Meister no. 40, word-decoded with
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R45_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`) and a scratch variant with a longer
name list and the 1/5 confusion; every break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and candidate words
force-aligned against them (`R45_corrections.tsv`). **Page order** follows the cipher's own catchwords (the transcriber
noted them; DECODE's image order is wrong): 359r, 359v (catchword 0 1 2 1 3 7 2 1 0 0 9 "nauarro" = 360r), 360r, 360v
(catchword 2 1 2 5 0 = 358r "a legato"), 358r, 358v (ends "suce-", continued by 361r "-dere ala corona"), 361r, 361v
(catchword 2 5 3 5 0 0 2 5 2 = 357r "[ri]cercase"), 357r. It is one letter. The DECODE "cleartext" images are a covering
letter in clear (ff. 355–356, Blois [?] January 1589) and its address leaf ("Bles … di Genaro … Card.le Morosino", with
a summary); not decipherments. The text dates itself after the Queen Mother's death (5 January 1589) and the recall of
Nevers. No image check was decisive (corroded leaves); corrections are `figures` / `figures+context`.
Spelling as the figures give it; punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re,
111 N. S., 116 Regina Madre, 129 duca di, 131 cardinale di, 132 principi, 133 arciuescouo, 135 uescouo/uescoui,
143 guerra, 146 danaro, 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 219 cifra, 226 catolico/
catolici, 227 heretico/heretici, 232 Re di Nauarra). m + 8 = -mente (longam., stretam., grauem., sicuram., quietam.,
compitam., totalm., animosam., altrim., falsam.). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 359r] […] se bene io desiderauo prima che ritornar[e] al'audientia del Re di aspetare qualche auiso da V. S. Ill.ma
per intendere da lei la mente di N. S. dapoi l'infelice sucesso dela morte de' signori cardinale et duca di Guisa, che
siano in gloria, tutauia, hauendo inteso che qui si ritrouaua un huomo mandato dal Re di Nauarra per tratare con S. M.tà
qualche acordo, et hauendo anco presentito che non uoleua uenire a quella dechiaratione che si era già stabilita contra
eso Nauarro, sicome ricercano tuti i Stati del regno, per non mancare io dal canto mio di fare tuto quello che io poso
per impedire che non segua cosa alcuna di pregiuditio ala religione catolica, non mi è parso lasare di procurare
audientia da S. M.tà; la quale, hauendomela hogi asignata, mi sono ritrouato seco asai longam[ente]. Et dopo hauere fato
seco quello oficio di condoglienza che conueniua per la morte dela Regina Madre, che sia in cielo, disi a S. M.tà che
l'ultima uolta che io le parlai ela stretam[ente] mi haueua pregato di scriuere a N. S., asicurando N. S. che più che mai
era risoluta di fare ogni sforzo per caciare l'heresia da questo regno, uolendo procedere con ogni rigore contra li
heretici, confiscare et uendere tuti i loro beni per seruirsi del danaro in proseguire la guerra contra di esi; che io
non haueuo mancato [f. 359v] di scriuerlo a V. S. Ill.ma perché ne potese dare conto a N. S.; ma che temeuo che mi
conuenise hora scriuere tuto in contrario, poiché intendeuo che S. M.tà non uoleua esequire quello che già haueua
promeso, cioè di dechiarare il Nauarro per heretico et incapace ala sucesione di questo regno, anzi di più che si
ritrouaua qui un huomo mandato da lui per tratare con la S. M.tà qualche acordo; il che, agiunto al hauere lei
richiamato l'esercito che faceua la guerra agli heretici per seruirsene contra quelli di Orliens, pareua a me che
ueniua a dare gran campo a quelli che mostrano di tenere la S. M.tà per poco catolica di comprobare con questi
argomenti molto bene la loro opinione; che però la pregauo a considerare molto bene quello che conueniua a [?un] Re
christianisimo et che faceua profesione di uero catolico, ricordandosi quanto è grande l'obligo che ela ha al sig. Dio,
che l'ha fata nascere così gran Re, et quanto ela deue procurare di placare l'ira di sua diuina Maestà, che deue esere
contra di lei grauem[ente] irritata per le cose pasate; che uolese considerare la mala sodisfatione che daria a tuti i
catolici del suo regno et di tuta la christianità quando lasciase di fare la dechiaratione che ha promesa contra eso
[f. 360r] Nauarro, perché faria sicuram[ente] credere il suo fine esere di uolere che egli dopo lei hauese a sucedere in
questo regno, cosa aborita da tuti i buoni, et che la S. M.tà più d'ogn'altro douria aborire per il proprio interese;
poiché, esendo eso Nauarro non solo heretico et inimico di Dio, ma che pretende anco di peruenire ala sucesione di
questa corona, non potrà mai la S. M.tà asicurarsi che egli, per potere più presto peruenire a tanta grandeza, non habia
ad insidiare la sua persona; et che quando non sia dechiarato inhabile et incapace ala sucesione haurà molto più seguito
che non hauria quando tuti sapesero che egli non potrà mai esere Re di Francia; et che di tratare acordo seco senza il
consenso di N. S. se ne guardase molto bene, perché quando lei uenise a questo io mi sarei subito partito di Francia, et
che mi perdonase se lo facesi senza andarmi a licentiare da lei; che la pregauo a considerare molto bene le cose sue,
guardandosi di non metere N. S. in necesità di fare ogni seuera dimostratione contra di lei, come io teneuo per certo
che faria quando uedese la S. M.tà, dopo le cose sucese, fare anco qualche altro impiastro con li heretici. Mi rispose
S. M.tà asai quietam[ente], se bene parue a me che si turbase in facia, et mi dise che quello [?mi] [f. 360v] haueua deto
di uolere più che mai proseguire la guerra contra gli heretici me lo tornaua a confirmare, et che speraua che gli efeti
comprobariano asai compitam[ente] questa sua ferma risolutione; et che il chiamare hora mons. di Niuers con quelle genti
non ripugnaua ala sua parola, perché questa era una necesità presente, ala quale d'altro modo non si poteua per adeso
rimediare, et che speraua di potere così presto spedirsi da questo bisogno che si saria stato in tempo ancora di fare
contra li heretici quello che hauea deto; che era uero che non uoleua fare quella dechiaratione contra il Re di Nauarra,
perché nel'edito dela pacificatione era già dechiarato che nisuno heretico potese sucedere a questa corona, il che
bastaua asai per escludere eso Nauarro senza uenire a più espresa dechiaratione contra la sua particolare persona,
perché questo saria meterlo in disperatione di non poter mai più farsi catolico, contra quello che io di ordine di
N. S. le haueuo deto, che bisognaua fare ogni opera per ridurlo al'obedientia di santa chiesa, come ela credeua che
ognuno douese desiderare; ma che egli hauese mandato huomo qui per tratar seco acordo, questo era falsisimo, et che
quando fose me lo diria certo, se non come [f. 358r] a legato, almeno come a suo amico; et che mi poteuo asicurare che
non farà mai acordo che prima non sia egli acordato con santa chiesa. Io replicai a S. M.tà che quanto a me haurei
desiderato che ela per altra uia, senza richiamare mons. di Niuers, hauese proueduto a suoi bisogni; et che quanto al
Nauarro mi pareua che douese esere così certa che mai egli posi esere buon catolico, che per questo rispeto non douria
restare di fare quella dechiaratione che ha promesa a tuti i suoi Stati et a tuto il mondo, leuando lui totalm[ente] dala
speranza et tuti i catolici dal timore che posi mai [pe]ruenire a questa corona; et che pareua a me che per ragione
politica ancora S. M.tà lo doueua in ogni modo fare, per leuargli il seguito et per asicurare la sua propria uita, contra
la quale più animosam[ente] [?conspirarà], [?sperando] di poter esere Re, che quando sarà certo di non potere esere. Mi
dise S. M.tà: "Uoglio parlarui chiaro in confidentia, sapendo che lo tenirete apreso di uoi, perché è cosa di
grandisima importanza, come ue ne prego. Sapiate che dopo la morte di questo di Guisa il cardinale di Uandomo et suoi
frateli si credono già di esere Re di Francia, et però hano operato che nel capitolo proposto da i Stati di escludere il
Re di Nauarra [f. 358v] ui si è agiunta una clausula importantisima, la quale è che, se bene quello è dichiarato
inhabile, si dice riseruando nondimeno il dirito dela sucesione a quelli dela casa di Borbone. Hor sapiate che, se a
loro apertiene di sucedere a questa corona, io non uoglio leuarli le loro ragioni; ma non uoglio meno aprouare […] che
restino confirmate nei Stati generali del regno, aciò non posino con questa sicureza dela sucesione insidiare ala mia
uita." Risposi a S. M.tà che se questa clausula le dispiaceua, che douria farla leuare et publicare il resto. Mi rispose
che questo non si potria far senza rumore et senza pericolo di soleuare anco questi contra di lei, doue che, leuando
insieme tuto il capitolo, non haueuano di che dolersi, parendo che questo fose più tosto in loro fauore che altrim[ente];
ma che haueua risoluto per altra uia di proseguire contra eso Re di Nauarra, perché il giorno seguente
uolea incorporare tuti i suoi beni ala corona come di ribele et heretico, che tanto ualerà quanto anco publicarlo per
quella altra uia. Al che replicai che, purché la S. M.tà facese la dichiaratione con il consenso dei Stati che egli resti
escluso in tuto di poter mai suce- [f. 361r] -dere ala corona come heretico et incapace, che non diceuo io che lo douese
fare più per una che per un'altra uia. Con che si terminò questo ragionamento, che fu asai più longo che qui non si dice
per scansare il tedio a V. S. Ill.ma.

Entrai poi a parlare di nuouo a S. M.tà sopra la publicatione del concilio, et l'esplicai quello apunto che si contiene
nela cifra di V. S. Ill.ma di [?5] del pasato, mostrandole la giusta indignatione di N. S. anco contra di me per le
conditioni che intendeua la S. M.tà di agiungere nela publicatione di eso concilio; che però io la pregauo et esortauo a
pensarui meglio et consigliarsi con persone inteligenti et timorose del sig. Dio, perché non trouaria alcuno catolico che
aprobase che i concili[i] generali confirmati dala santa sede apostolica posino esere in questo modo mutilati da
qualsiuoglia Re o principe per grande che sia; et che quando la S. M.tà continouase nela prima risolutione daria grande
ocasione a quelli che non l'amano di comprobare con questo argomento che ela non habia quello zelo ala religione
catolica che conuiene ad un Re christianis[imo], et che per un'ombra falsa d'interese dela sua autorità ueniria a perdere
la più bela ocasione che se le posi presentare di mostrare ala Santità di N. S. et al mondo tuto come falsam[ente] uenga
la S. M.tà [f. 361v] imputata nele cose dela religione; doue facendo in contrario non solo doueua temere la giusta ira di
Dio, ma anco l'indignatione di N. S. et la mala opinione di tuto il christianesmo; che io, nel dispiacere che sentirò
dele auersità che per questo le posono sucedere, haurò nela propria conscienza questo refrigerio di sapere almeno di
non hauere mancato in uoce molte uolte et in scrito ancora di ricordarle quello che per debito di conscienza et per
utilità dele cose sue è tenuta di fare in questo proposito. Et dopo le mandai un memoriale del medesmo tenore, che lo
facese legere nel suo consiglio, insieme con una scritura fata ad instanza del uescouo di [?Eureus] et sotoscrita da
molti uescoui et altri dei Stati generali, che dicono che il concilio si deue publicare senza alcuna conditione. Mi
rispose S. M.tà che non mancaria di considerare sopra quello che io le diceuo; ma che le pareua che dele conditioni
"saluis iuribus regis et regni" io me ne douesi contentare. Disi a la S. M.tà che lei douea publicare il concilio come
stà et giace, senza altra conditione, come hano fato tuti gli altri Re et principi catolici, che non manco di lei
uogliono conseruare la loro autorità; et se pretende alcuna riserua, che acetando il concilio ne ri- [f. 357r] -cercase
N. S., che, come molte uolte per nome dela [Santità di] N. S. le haueuo deto, saria in tute le cose honeste compiaciuta.
La S. M.tà non mi rispose altro, et io mi licentiai. Ho uoluto dire questo tuto a V. S. Ill.ma perché la resti informata
di tuto quello che pasa, se bene io non so se haurò fato bene o male, considerando quello che la mi scriue nela sodeta sua
cifra, doue mi dice che non […] mi laso dare la burla, o che mi sodisfo di discorsi. Quanto ala burla, [?non] mi tengo
per tanto soficiente che non mi posi esere data; ma quanto a discorsi, pare a me di non far altro nele mie ma che
rapresentare a V. S. Ill.ma il uero di tuto quello che pasa; et se in ciò io non sodisfo al suo desiderio, può esere certa
che molto me ne duole et ne sento estremo dispiacere; ma la suplico a credere che io non saprei fare meglio, et che non ho
magiore desiderio che di seruire bene, né penso ad altro il giorno et la note. Ma se non sucedono le cose come ela
uorria, so che per la molta sua prudenza conosce che in mano mia non è di potere far fare al Re di Francia quello che egli
non uole. Si uano formando i procesi contra questi sig. di Guisa, et l'altra matina mandarono dui consiglieri per
esaminare l'arciuescouo [di] Lione; ma egli dise che, esendo arciuescouo et primato di Francia, non poteua esere
esaminato da laici; et io ancora feci intendere a S. M.tà che se ne astenese, come ha fato […].

## Notes on the figures

- 359r l. 1: the opening "4 4 5 2 2 7 0 0 1" (before "8 se bene") does not parse; the letter may begin on a lost leaf.
- 359v l. 12: "a 7 9 8 2 1 2 0 0 3 5 christianisimo": "[?un] Re" (79 is "come").
- 358r l. 15: "conspirarà" 1 9 4 4 1 7 0 0 2 1 0 0 2 9 9 (ending not as the key spells it), "sperando" 4 6 4 1 7 1 2 6 7
  (s + per + i d i); both partly carried.
- 358v l. 6: "aprouare 0 5 1 7 1 9 1 6 che restino": the object is not carried.
- 361r l. 6: "di 8 5 del pasato": the day of Montalto's cipher; read 5 after a null 8 (plain-figure dates and sums are
  closed or opened by an 8 in this series).
- 361v l. 12: "uescouo di 8 1 7 3 7 0 0 3 7 4 5": "Eurus" — Évreux (Claude de Sainctes) is the likely see; not settled.
- 357r l. 1: "dela 111": "dela [Santità di] N. S." (the code alone is carried).
- 357r l. 7: "che non 9 1 9 8 mi laso": two figures before "mi" not carried.
- 357r l. 24: the closing "2 7 111. 4 2 0 0 1 7 1 0 2 2" after "come ha fato" does not parse.

R45_en.md

# R45 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Blois, [mid-]January 1589: audience with Henry III on Navarre, Nevers, the Council of Trent)

Translation of `R45_reading.md` (pages in the cipher's catchword order); holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 359r] […] although I wished, before returning to audience with the King, to wait for some word from Your Most
Illustrious Lordship to learn Our Lord's mind after the unhappy event of the deaths of the Cardinal and the Duke of Guise
(may they be in glory), nevertheless, having heard that a man sent by the King of Navarre was here to negotiate some
accord with His Majesty, and having also learned beforehand that he would not come to the declaration already settled
against Navarre, as all the Estates of the kingdom demand, so as not to fail on my side to do all I can to prevent
anything prejudicial to the Catholic religion, I thought I should not fail to seek audience of His Majesty. He granted
it me today, and I was with him a long time. After making the office of condolence fitting for the death of the Queen
Mother (may she be in heaven), I told His Majesty that the last time I spoke with him he had earnestly begged me to
write to Our Lord assuring him that he was more than ever resolved to make every effort to drive heresy out of this
kingdom, meaning to proceed with all rigour against the heretics, to confiscate and sell all their goods and use the
money to pursue the war against them; that I had not failed [f. 359v] to write this to Your Lordship so that you could
report it to Our Lord; but that I feared I must now write the very opposite, since I heard that His Majesty would not
carry out what he had promised, namely to declare Navarre a heretic and incapable of the succession to this kingdom, and
moreover that a man sent by him was here to negotiate an accord with His Majesty; which, added to his having recalled
the army that was making war on the heretics in order to use it against the people of Orléans, seemed to me to give
great scope to those who show they hold His Majesty to be a poor Catholic to prove their opinion very well by these
arguments. Therefore I begged him to consider carefully what befitted [a] Most Christian King who professed to be a true
Catholic, remembering how great is his obligation to the Lord God, who had him born so great a king, and how much he
must seek to appease the wrath of His Divine Majesty, which must be gravely provoked against him by past events; to
consider the ill satisfaction he would give all the Catholics of his kingdom and of all Christendom if he failed to make
the declaration he has promised against the said [f. 360r] Navarre, for it would surely make people believe that his
aim was that Navarre should succeed him in this kingdom — a thing abhorred by all good men, and which His Majesty more
than anyone ought to abhor in his own interest; since, Navarre being not only a heretic and enemy of God but also
claiming the succession to this crown, His Majesty could never be safe from his plotting against his person to reach
such greatness sooner; and that unless he were declared unfit and incapable of the succession he would have a much
larger following than if everyone knew he could never be King of France; and that he should take great care not to
negotiate an accord with him without Our Lord's consent, because if he came to that I would leave France at once, and
he must forgive me if I did it without coming to take leave of him. I begged him to consider his affairs carefully,
taking care not to put Our Lord under the necessity of making every severe demonstration against him, as I held it
certain he would if he saw His Majesty, after what had happened, make some other patched-up arrangement with the
heretics. His Majesty answered me quite calmly, though it seemed to me his face was troubled, and told me that what he
[f. 360v] had said about wanting more than ever to pursue the war against the heretics he confirmed again, and hoped the
effects would prove this firm resolve of his quite fully; that recalling Monsieur de Nevers with those troops now was
not contrary to his word, because this was a present necessity which could not be remedied otherwise for now, and he
hoped to be done with this need so soon that there would still be time to do against the heretics what he had said;
that it was true he would not make that declaration against the King of Navarre, because in the Edict of Pacification it
was already declared that no heretic could succeed to this crown, which was quite enough to exclude Navarre without a
more express declaration against his particular person, since that would drive him to despair of ever becoming a
Catholic — contrary to what I, by Our Lord's order, had told him, that every effort must be made to bring him back to
the obedience of Holy Church, as he believed everyone ought to wish; but that Navarre had sent a man here to negotiate an
accord was utterly false, and that if it were so he would certainly tell me, if not as [f. 358r] legate, at least as his
friend; and that I could be sure he would never make an accord before Navarre was reconciled with Holy Church. I
replied to His Majesty that for my part I would have wished him to provide for his needs some other way, without
recalling Monsieur de Nevers; and that as to Navarre, it seemed to me he should be so certain Navarre could never be a
good Catholic that he ought not on that account to refrain from making the declaration he had promised to all his
Estates and to the whole world, taking away from Navarre all hope, and from all Catholics the fear, that he might ever
come to this crown; and that it seemed to me that for reasons of policy too His Majesty ought by all means to do it, to
take away his following and to secure his own life, against which Navarre would [conspire] more boldly, [hoping] he
might be King, than when he is sure he cannot be. His Majesty said to me: "I want to speak plainly to you in confidence,
knowing you will keep it to yourself, for it is a matter of very great importance, as I beg you. Know that after the
death of this Guise the Cardinal of Vendôme and his brothers already believe themselves Kings of France, and so they have
contrived that in the article proposed by the Estates to exclude the King of Navarre [f. 358v] a most important clause
has been added, which is that, although he is declared unfit, the right of succession is nevertheless reserved to those
of the House of Bourbon. Now know that if the succession to this crown belongs to them, I do not want to take their
rights from them; but neither do I want to approve […] that they be confirmed in the Estates General of the kingdom, so
that with this security of the succession they cannot plot against my life." I answered His Majesty that if this clause
displeased him he should have it removed and publish the rest. He answered that this could not be done without uproar
and without danger of raising these men too against him, whereas by removing the whole article together they had nothing
to complain of, since this seemed rather in their favour than otherwise; but that he had resolved to proceed against the
King of Navarre by another way, since the next day he meant to annex all his goods to the crown as a rebel and heretic,
which would be worth as much as publishing it by that other way. To which I replied that provided His Majesty made the
declaration, with the consent of the Estates, that he remain wholly excluded from ever succeeding [f. 361r] to the crown
as a heretic and incapable, I did not say it must be done by one way rather than another. With this the conversation
ended; it was much longer than is told here, to spare Your Lordship tedium.

I then spoke again to His Majesty about the publication of the Council, and set out to him exactly what is contained in
Your Lordship's cipher of the [5th?] of last month, showing him Our Lord's just indignation, against me as well, at the
conditions His Majesty meant to add to the publication of the Council; and so I begged and exhorted him to think it over
and take counsel with intelligent and God-fearing persons, for he would find no Catholic who would approve that general
councils confirmed by the Holy Apostolic See could be mutilated in this way by any king or prince however great; and
that if His Majesty persisted in his first resolution he would give great occasion to those who do not love him to prove
by this argument that he has not the zeal for the Catholic religion befitting a Most Christian King, and that for a false
shadow of interest in his authority he would lose the finest occasion that could be offered him to show His Holiness and
the whole world how falsely His Majesty [f. 361v] is accused in matters of religion; whereas by doing the contrary he
would have to fear not only the just wrath of God but also Our Lord's indignation and the ill opinion of all
Christendom; and that in the grief I shall feel at the adversities that may befall him for this, I shall have in my own
conscience this comfort, at least to know I did not fail, by word many times and in writing too, to remind him of what he
is bound to do in this matter by duty of conscience and for the good of his affairs. Afterwards I sent him a memorial to
the same effect, that he might have it read in his council, together with a paper drawn up at the instance of the Bishop
of [Évreux?] and signed by many bishops and others of the Estates General, who say the Council must be published without
any condition. His Majesty answered that he would not fail to consider what I told him; but that it seemed to him I
ought to be content with the conditions *saluis iuribus regis et regni*. I told His Majesty that he ought to publish the
Council as it stands, without other condition, as all the other Catholic kings and princes have done, who no less than
he wish to preserve their authority; and if he claims some reservation, that in accepting the Council he should ask it
[f. 357r] of Our Lord, who, as I had told him many times in His Holiness's name, would oblige him in all honest things.
His Majesty answered nothing more, and I took my leave. I have wished to tell all this to Your Lordship so that you may
remain informed of everything that happens, though I do not know whether I shall have done well or ill, considering what
you write me in your said cipher, where you tell me that I […] let myself be fooled, or that I content myself with talk.
As to being fooled, I do not hold myself so able that it could not happen to me; but as to talk, it seems to me I do
nothing in my letters but represent to Your Lordship the truth of all that happens; and if in this I do not satisfy your
wish, you may be sure it grieves me much and I feel extreme displeasure; but I beg you to believe that I could not do
better, and that I have no greater wish than to serve well, nor think of anything else day and night. But if things do
not turn out as you would wish, I know that in your great prudence you understand that it is not in my hand to make the
King of France do what he will not. The trials against these Guise lords are being prepared, and the other morning they
sent two councillors to examine the Archbishop of Lyon; but he said that, being archbishop and primate of France, he
could not be examined by laymen; and I too let His Majesty know that he should refrain from it, as he has done […].

R46, Francia 22/25, Blois, 24 Jan 1589 (dup.)

The Pope rejects the clause "saluis iuribus regis et regni", and Morosini works on the King's confessor and the Keeper of the Seals, who promise to argue his case. Saluzzo is set aside for now. At length Morosini complains of the Pope's displeasure and the false reports reaching Rome, and he begs leave to come to Rome to justify himself.

# R46 — Morosini to Montalto, [Blois, 24 January 1589]: the publication of the Council of Trent; the Pope's displeasure (Francia 22/25, ff. 381r–384r)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1711 (KaJo, Dec 2015) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R46_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops; `R46_corrections.tsv`).
One line was re-read from the image (382r l. 12, where the transcription repeats the end of l. 13):
`R46_transcription_corrected.txt`. No date in cipher. Tempesti, *Vita di Sisto V* (1754) II, book IX, quotes part of
this letter as Morosini's "cifra de' 24 Gennaro" [1589] (the complaint of the Pope's displeasure, 382v), and just before
it Montalto's cipher of 16 December 1588 that this letter answers ("saluis iuribus regis et regni … la maledice … uisum
est Spiritui Sancto et nobis"); Tempesti was used to recognise sense only, not as a source of words. No
contemporary decipherment on the DECODE images (the two "cleartext" images are despatches in clear).
Page order: 381r–382v, then 383r–384r. The catchword at the foot of 382v (2 1 5 0 9 1 1) does not match the first
figures of 383r, so a leaf is probably missing between them; 384r ends in mid-sentence.
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes
expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma,
196 Sauoia, 216 auiso, 219 cifra, 221 lettera).
Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [word] supplied.

## Reading

[f. 381r] […] con l'ultime mie non hebi tempo di rispondere ale cifre di V. S. Ill.ma di 24 del pasato, hora le dico
che, hauendo inteso quanto la mi scriue intorno al concilio di Trento, feci subito sapere al Re che N. S. non solo non
aceta la clausula "saluis iuribus regis et regni", ma che la maledice; che però io esortauo S. M.tà, che quel giorno
haueua risoluto di publicare questo nei Stati, che non lo douese fare se non liberam[ente], senza alcuna conditione,
perché altrim[enti] facendo ofenderia Dio, con il quale non s'ha da far patti, et daria mala sodisfatione a N. S. et a
tuta la christianità; ricordandole che le parole de' concili generali sono parole di Dio, perché dicono i padri "uisum
est Spiritui Sancto et nobis", [?et] replicandole in sostanza quello che molte altre uolte le haueuo deto et scrito, a
V. S. Ill.ma con l'ultime mie. Sopra di che, hauendo di nuouo considerato S. M.tà, lasciò di publi[c]are nei Stati questo
punto, ma dise che, quanto ala publicatione di eso concilio, ela uoleua in ogni modo che fose publicato et acetato, et
così le faceua intendere, che per tale lo tenesero; ma, che non esendo ancora ben risolute alcune dificoltà di
riserue che erano pr[f. 381v]oposte da esi Stati, uoleua hauerui ancora sopra più matura consideratione, et che le
risolueria insieme con gl'altri capitoli, che per la breuità del tempo non si erano ancora potuti terminare. Io poi,
per scarico dela mia conscienza, se bene mi scriue V. S. Ill.ma che non me ne pigli altro fastidio, credendo nondimeno
che il desiderio suo fose di uedere bene terminato questo negotio per gloria di Dio et beneficio di questo regno, non
ho mancato con l'abate di Sanlis, confesore di S. M.tà, con il guarda sigilo et con tuti quei altri che hanno seco
autorità di fare ogni eficace oficio per esortarli a persuaderla di publicarlo senza alcuna conditione; et pare a me
di hauere in ogni modo fato qualche fruto, perché hieri mi mandò S. M.tà a casa il guarda sigilo insieme con il suo
confesore, che per nome suo mi disero che, hauendo S. M.tà considerato sopra i memoriali che in questo proposito le
haueuo mandati, hauria molto desiderato di truouare modo di sodisfarmi senza dare mala sodisfatione a tuto il suo
regno, [?et] che pregaua [?dar] […] [f. 382r] ocasione a N. S. di procurare con l'autorità sua di farla obedire da'
suoi uasali in cosa tanto giusta et ragioneuole. Mostrarono loro di restare molto capaci di quello che li diceuo, et
partirono con prometermi di dire al Re che le mie ragioni erano bonisime et che S. M.tà così doueua fare. Hora stano
aspetando la risolutione, et ne darò auiso a V. S. Ill.ma.

Quanto ale cose di Saluzo, per hora non mi ocore altro, poiché questi ultimi sucesi tengono ocupata S. M.tà in altri
pensieri, che al presente più le premono.

Et quanto di non hauere io dato mai auiso dela riceuta dela copia di quella lettera del Serenis.[mo] di Sauoia
[?scrita] a V. S. Ill.ma, che mi inuiò con le sue di tre di otobre, credo che le sue molte ocupationi non le hanno
lasato auertire che nele medesme cifre di 1[8?] di Nouembre, ale quali mi risponde con questa medesma cifra, se ne fa
mentione, oltre quello che le acusai nele mie di 23 d'otobre in risposta dele sue di tre del medesmo mese. Quello che a
me in estremo duole è di uedere in questa sua cifra, come anco in alcuna dele [f. 382v] precedenti, che N. S. si
mostra mal sodisfato di me, senza potermi io imaginare la causa; et molto più mi preme che di già questo rumore è anco
peruenuto per sino al'orechie del Re et di questa corte, esendo stato scrito a S. M.tà alcuni particolari fastidiosi
[…] tanto lontani non solo dal uero ma anco dal posibile, che io resto più che certo che né V. S. Ill.ma né meno N. S.,
che è piena di tanta prudenza et di così raro et isquisito giuditio, posi hauere [?le] prestata alcuna sorte di fede.
Et se bene le ationi mie di molti ani posono apreso tuto il mondo scaricarmi da così fate imposture, tutauia riceuerò
anco per singolare gratia da N. S. che gli piacia di concedermi che io quanto prima posi uenire a i suoi santis[imi]
piedi per giustificare tute le ationi mie, perché, con il fauore del sig. Dio, spero che conoscerà asai chiaram[ente]
che io l'ho seruito con tanta fedeltà, sincerità et deuotione quanto si posi desiderare in qualsiuoglia altro
ministro, il quale, se bene hauese potuto seruire con magior […] [f. 383r] […]ere magiore autorità et dominio che
sopra di me. Se poi riesce dela legatione mia quello fruto che aspetaua N. S., la suplico a considerare se il
mancamento uiene da me o da […], né uoglia per l'amore di Dio atribuire a me le colpe che non sono mie et darmi la pena
de' pecati altrui. A me non duole meno questo che a N. S.; ma consideri lei se mai mi ha comandata cosa che io
prontam[ente] non l'habia esequita, et se mai per rispeto di chi si sia io habia lasciato di seruire fedelm[ente] a
N. S., procurando sempre con tuti li spiriti et con ogni uiueza la conseruatione dela riputatione et dignità sua,
sperando di potere con questi mezi farmi degno dela sua buona gratia et di conseruare quel poca di riputatione che con
le fatiche di molti ani ho procurato d'aquistarmi, la quale io confeso di stimare più che la propria uita. Però,
uedendomi senza alcuna mia colpa, col fare il meglio ch'ho saputo, a questo mal termine del'uno et del'altro, conuengo
uiuere scons[f. 383v]olatisimo sino a tanto che piacia a N. S. che io uenga a la presenza sua per giustificare le
ationi mie; […] prego con ogni afeto V. S. Ill.ma di adoprarsi per farmi otenire questa licenza, perché non solo farà
gratia a me, ma anco seruitio a cotesta santa Sede, esendo che, se io sino a qui ho fato poco fruto mentre che il Re
[?et] il regno pensauano che io hauesi credito et qualche autorità apreso N. S., hora che sono persuasi del contrario
conuenir[à] a esere molto meno, né faranno alcuna stima di me, poiché tuta quella che si faceua tuta nasceua per il
reflesso dela buona gratia di N. S. […] Et per dire il uero io non saprei come più sapere seruire, uedendo che con il
fare meglio che ho saputo ho nondimeno disgustato tanto N. S., che mostra anco di restare mal sodisfata di quello che
con ogni fedeltà scriuo dele cose che peruengono a mia notitia; onde nel auenire, sempre che mi uenirà ocasione di
scriuere qualche cosa o di Saluzo o d'altro, conuenirà et scriuen[f. 384r]do et tacendo temer sempre di far dispiacere a
N. S. Suplico V. S. Ill.ma a discusarmi se l'ho fastidita con questa longa diceria, considerando che a ciò
mi ha spinto l'estremo dispiacere che io sento di uedere in tanto pericolo quello che sopra tute le cose del mondo
stimo, che è la buona gratia di N. S., insieme con il mio honore. Racomando dunque a V. S. Ill.ma l'un[o] et l'altro
con ogni afeto, per sostenere una creatura sua che non mancarà mai di adoprarsi in suo seruitio, pregandola a credere
che io non mi sono moso a scriuerle per uolere hauer ragione alcuna con N. S., perché da lei non desidero altro che
quello solo che le piace, ma perché sia informata dela uerità et posi sincerare l'animo dela Santità di N. S., quando
da persone di poca conscientia fose altram[ente] auisata […]

# R46 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Blois, 24 January 1589]: the Council of Trent; the Pope's displeasure)

Translation of `R46_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 381r] […] with my last letters I had no time to answer Your Most Illustrious Lordship's ciphers of the 24th of last
month. Now I tell you that, having understood what you write me about the Council of Trent, I at once let the King know
that Our Lord not only does not accept the clause "saving the rights of the King and of the kingdom", but curses it;
and so I urged His Majesty, who had resolved that day to publish this in the Estates, not to do it except freely and
without any condition, because doing otherwise he would offend God, with whom one does not make bargains, and would
give dissatisfaction to Our Lord and to all Christendom; reminding him that the words of general councils are words of
God, for the Fathers say "it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us", [and] repeating to him in substance what I had
told him and written many other times, to Your Most Illustrious Lordship with my last letters. On this His Majesty,
having considered again, left off publishing this point in the Estates, but said that, as for the publication of the
said council, he wanted it in any case to be published and accepted, and was letting them know so, that they should
hold it as such; but that, since certain difficulties about reservations [f. 381v] put forward by those Estates were
not yet well resolved, he wanted to give them still riper consideration, and would resolve them together with the
other articles, which for shortness of time had not yet been settled. I then, to discharge my conscience — although
Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes me not to trouble myself further about it, believing nonetheless that your wish
was to see this business well concluded for the glory of God and the good of this kingdom — have not failed to do every
effective office with the Abbé of Senlis, His Majesty's confessor, with the Keeper of the Seals and with all those others
who have authority with him, urging them to persuade him to publish it without any condition; and it seems to me that
I have in any case had some result, for yesterday His Majesty sent the Keeper of the Seals to my house together with his
confessor, who told me in his name that His Majesty, having considered the memorials I had sent him on this matter,
would much have wished to find a way of satisfying me without displeasing his whole kingdom, [and] that he begged […]
[f. 382r] occasion for Our Lord to work, with his authority, to make him obeyed by his vassals in so just and reasonable
a matter. They showed themselves well persuaded of what I told them, and left promising to tell the King that my
reasons were excellent and that His Majesty ought to do so. They are now awaiting his resolution, and I shall send word
of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

As for the affairs of Saluzzo, I have nothing more for now, since these latest events keep His Majesty busy with other
thoughts that press him more at present.

And as to my never having acknowledged receipt of the copy of the letter of His Most Serene Highness of Savoy [written]
to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, which you sent me with yours of the third of October, I think your many occupations
have not let you notice that in my very ciphers of the 1[8th?] of November, to which you answer with this same cipher,
it is mentioned, besides what I acknowledged in mine of the 23rd of October in answer to yours of the third of the same
month. What grieves me extremely is to see in this cipher of yours, as also in some of the [f. 382v] preceding ones,
that Our Lord shows himself ill satisfied with me, without my being able to imagine the cause; and it presses me much
more that this rumour has already reached the ears of the King and of this court, certain vexatious particulars having
been written to His Majesty […] so far not only from the truth but even from the possible that I remain more than
certain that neither Your Most Illustrious Lordship nor still less Our Lord, who is full of such prudence and of such
rare and exquisite judgement, could have given [them] any kind of credence. And although my actions of many years can
clear me before the whole world of such impostures, nevertheless I shall receive it as a singular grace from Our Lord
if it please him to grant me to come as soon as possible to his most holy feet to justify all my actions; for, with the
favour of the Lord God, I hope he will see quite clearly that I have served him with as much fidelity, sincerity and
devotion as could be wished in any other minister, who, although he could have served with greater […] [f. 383r] […]
greater authority and dominion than over me. If then the fruit Our Lord expected from my legation does not […] come,
I beg you to consider whether the fault comes from me or from […], and not, for the love of God, to lay on me faults
that are not mine and give me the penalty of others' sins. This grieves me no less than Our Lord; but let you consider
whether he has ever commanded me anything that I did not promptly carry out, and whether for regard of anyone at all I
have ever failed to serve Our Lord faithfully, always working with all my spirit and all my vigour for the preservation
of his reputation and dignity, hoping by these means to make myself worthy of his good grace and to keep the little
reputation that I have tried to win with the labours of many years, which I confess I value more than my own life.
Therefore, seeing myself, through no fault of mine and while doing the best I knew, in this bad state with the one and
with the other, I must live most disconsolate [f. 383v] until it please Our Lord that I come into his presence to
justify my actions; […] I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship with all my heart to work to obtain this leave for me,
since you will do not only a favour to me but a service to that Holy See: for if until now I have done little good
while the King [and] the kingdom thought I had credit and some authority with Our Lord, now that they are persuaded of
the contrary it will have to be much less, and they will take no account of me, since all the esteem there was came
wholly from the reflection of Our Lord's good grace […] And to tell the truth I would not know how to serve any better,
seeing that, doing the best I knew, I have nevertheless so displeased Our Lord that he even shows himself ill satisfied
with what I write in all fidelity of the things that come to my knowledge; so that in future, whenever I have occasion
to write anything, about Saluzzo or anything else, I shall have, both in writing and in keeping [f. 384r] silent, always
to fear displeasing Our Lord. I beg Your Most Illustrious Lordship to excuse me if I have wearied you with this long
discourse, considering that I was driven to it by the extreme distress I feel at seeing in such danger what I value
above everything in the world, which is the good grace of Our Lord, together with my honour. I commend, then, to Your
Most Illustrious Lordship the one and the other with all my heart, in order to sustain a creature of yours who will
never fail to work in your service, begging you to believe that I have not been moved to write to you in order to be
in the right against Our Lord — for from him I desire nothing but what pleases him — but so that you may be informed of
the truth and may set His Holiness's mind at rest, should he be informed otherwise by persons of little conscience […]

R47, Francia 22/26, n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589]

Morosini continues his defence and denies ever dealing with the English ambassador. He explains why the Council could not be forced through the parlements and the Estates. He had suggested that the King publish it at once and then send a personage to Rome to ask for his privileges.

# R47 — Morosini to Montalto, n.d. [Blois, January 1589] (two leaves of a longer letter): the Council and his own defence (Francia 22/26, ff. 386r–v, 385r–v)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1712 (KaJo, Dec 2015) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R47_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures (`R47_corrections.tsv`). No "cleartext" images are attached to this record on DECODE; no glosses.
Page order: DECODE's transcriber noted that "page order might be wrong" from the catchwords. 386r begins inside a word
("[cons]iderare") and the catchword at the foot of 385v ("3 2 3 5 0 0 5 2 0 2", = "uere ma-") does not
match 386r, so the leaf that followed 385v is not in the record. 386v ends "et dare" and 385r begins "a lo Re ...": this
reading puts 386r–v before 385r–v, which gives continuous sense, but the junction is not certain. Undated; it belongs
with R46 (Blois, 24 Jan 1589), where Morosini defends his conduct and asks leave to come to Rome.
Spelling as the figures give it; punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes expanded (111 N. S., 113 S. M.tà /
il Re, 132 principe, 161 quanto, 165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 173 Inghilterra, 213
ambasciatore). Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 386r] […][cons]iderare, che in questi tempi turbulenti conueniua andare con molti rispeti, temendo che, quando anco
lei hauese uoluto comandare al parlamento di publicare senza alcuna riserua eso concilio, che loro non l'hauriano
ubedita, perché, come io sapeuo, tuti tre gli ordini dei stati generali ne dimandauano qualcheduna. Che però, hauendo
lei con più uolte deto che N. S. non intendeua per questo di leuare i suoi priuilegi né le prerogatiue del regno, et mi
dimandaua se io truouauo buono che la S. M.tà mandase a Roma un personagio per rimostrare a N. S. i capi doue si toca
la sua autorità, pregandola che le piacese di riseruarli, perché quando questo si fose fato publicaria poi il concilio
senza altra conditione o riserua, io le disi che a uoler fare bene et aquistare gratia con N. S. bisognaua adeso,
senza altra dilatione, publicare il concilio nel modo isteso che è stato publicato in tuto il [?resto] dela
christianità, et mandar poi il personagio a Roma per dimandare [f. 386v] a N. S. quelle gratie et quei priuilegi che
desideraua, prometendole io in nome di N. S., conforme agli ordini mandatimi da V. S. Ill.ma, che in tute le cose
honeste et ragioneuoli saria compiaciuta. Mi disero che temeuano che questo forse imposibile di poter fare in quel
modo, perché né i popoli né i parlamenti l'acetariano. Io li risposi che né i popoli né i parlam[enti] sono chiamati
ala celebratione de' concili, ma solamente i prelati, a' quali [?aperteneua] d'insegnare agl' altri non meno la dotrina
che i costumi, et che quando ciò era confirmato dala santa sede apostolica non conueniua a popoli altra consideratione,
ma solo oseruare gli ordini et le constitutioni terminate, perché in tanto è buono et uero quello che uediamo nela
nostra fede in quanto ci uiene comandato et insegnato dala chiesa; et che però non doueua S. M.tà per questo rispeto
lasare di publicare eso concilio, perché, [se] i popoli non la uolesero in questo obedire, ela almeno hauria dal canto suo
complito a quello che è tenuta et obligata, et dare [f. 385r] a lo Re […]. Et con più prudenza di me non lo poteua
certo, né con magior ardore né con magior fede, non hauendo io mai hauta altra mira che l'honore del Sig. Dio, il buon
seruitio di N. S. et di cotesta santa sede.

Et se ben so che qualcheduno si mostra mal sodisfato di me perché io habia hauto più consideratione al'obligo mio che a'
desideri loro, et lo reputo nondimeno a mio magior honore, poiché questo suceso per hauere io senza rispeto d'altri
uoluto sempre ben seruire al mio padrone, dela dignità del quale più si trata nela [?destratione] che si fa a me ala
presenza sua et dela mia propria. Né questa mala sodisfatione d'altri mi ha potuto mai deuiare di non continouare
sempre nel medesmo proposito di ben seruire il mio principe, perché oltre a gli mortali oblighi che gli tengo, per causa
de' quali spenderò sempre la propria uita, è anco uicario di Christo, che può bastare ad ogni christiano per farlo
caminare nel suo seruitio con quella medesma fede et uerità che faria con l'isteso Signore, che uede l'intrinsico
[f. 385v] de' nostri cuori. Però quando N. S. truouarà in me, non dico l'enorme et esecrabile mancamento di hauere
tenuto pratiche con l'ambasciatore d'Inghilterra, il quale né conosco né so mai di hauere ueduto, come sono auisato
et come uiene scrito al medesmo Re esere stato deto a N. S., ma qualsiuoglia altro minimo mancamento che per malitia
habia comeso nel suo seruitio, la suplico a non hauere di me alcuna pietà o misericordia, ma castigarmi con i più
[?aspri] et seueri castighi che si posino dare al più scelerato huomo del mondo; [?però] io, se non mi inganno,
crederei che né apreso V. S. Ill.ma né apreso N. S. douese alcuno hauere hauta più fede di me, poiché non c'è alcuno
che gli sia più obligato, oltre che credo di eser stato per gratia del Signor Dio da tuti quelli c'hano hauto
pratica di me conosciuto per alienisimo dal uitio del'ingratitudine; et quando V. S. Ill.ma uorrà far proua dela
mia fede et gratitudine, conoscerà di non hauere alcuno a questo mondo sopra di che posi ha[uere ma-] […]

## Notes on the figures

- "[?resto]" (386r l. 19): "8 3? 3 5 4 5 9": the transcriber's 3? may be 13 (r); "resto" would be 13 5 47 9.
- "[?imposibile]" (386v l. 5): 1 7 1 2 9 9 1 5 4 1 7 4 2 1 7 5 0 5, one 9 too many and no p (29 = mp stands for it).
- "[?aperteneua]" (386v l. 9): 2 6 4 1 5 3 5 0 1 3 5 3 7 0 2 1 2 = a per te ne u (0) a; one stray 0.
- "et dare [f. 385r] a lo Re […]": the junction of the two leaves (see header); "a lo Re" is 21 50 91 13 5.
- 385r l. 1: "non lo poteua certo" — a verb (fare) is not in the figures.
- "[?destratione]" (385r l. 11): 2 6 3 5 4 9 2 1 5 1 1 7 9 1 0 1 5 = de str atione; "dimostratione" would need 20 91.
- "[?aspri]" (385v l. 10): 2 4 6 1 7 1 = a + "4 6" + i; aspri would be 2 44 13 171.
- "[?però] io" (385v l. 11): 6 4 1 5 3 1 7 1 9 = per + e + io.
- The last words "sopra di che posi ha-" run into the catchword "uere ma-"; the following leaf is missing.

# R47 — English (Morosini to Montalto, n.d. [Blois, January 1589], two leaves of a longer letter: the Council and his own defence)

Translation of `R47_reading.md`; holes as there. The order of the two leaves (386r–v before 385r–v) is the reading's,
not certain.

## Translation

[f. 386r] […] to consider that in these turbulent times one had to proceed with many regards, fearing that, even if he
had chosen to order the Parlement to publish the said council without any reservation, they would not have obeyed him,
because, as I knew, all three orders of the Estates General were asking for some reservation. Therefore, he having said
several times that Our Lord did not mean by this to remove his privileges or the prerogatives of the kingdom, and asking
me whether I thought it good that His Majesty should send a personage to Rome to show Our Lord the heads in which his
authority is touched, begging him to be pleased to reserve them, because once this was done he would then publish the
council without any other condition or reservation — I told him that, to do well and gain favour with Our Lord, he must
now, without further delay, publish the council in the same manner in which it has been published in all the [rest] of
Christendom, and then send the personage to Rome to ask [f. 386v] Our Lord for the graces and privileges he desired,
promising him in Our Lord's name, in accordance with the orders sent me by Your Most Illustrious Lordship, that in all
honest and reasonable things he would be satisfied. They told me they feared this was perhaps impossible to do in that
way, because neither the people nor the parlements would accept it. I answered them that neither the people nor the
parlements are called to the celebration of councils, but only the prelates, to whom [it belonged] to teach the others
doctrine no less than morals; and that when this was confirmed by the Holy Apostolic See the people had no other
consideration to make than to observe the orders and constitutions laid down, because what we see in our faith is good
and true in so far as it is commanded and taught us by the Church; and that therefore His Majesty ought not on this
account to fail to publish the said council, because, [if] the people would not obey him in this, he at least would have
done his part in what he is bound and obliged to do, and to give [f. 385r] to the King […]. And he certainly could not
[do it] with more prudence than I, nor with greater ardour nor greater fidelity, since I have never had any other aim
than the honour of the Lord God and the good service of Our Lord and of that Holy See.

And although I know that someone shows himself dissatisfied with me because I have had more regard for my duty than
for their wishes, I nevertheless count it to my greater honour, since this happened because I, without regard for
others, always chose to serve my master well, whose dignity is more at stake in the [treatment] given to me in his
presence and in my own. Nor has this dissatisfaction of others ever been able to turn me from continuing always in the
same purpose of serving my prince well, because, besides the deadly obligations I have to him, for which I shall always
spend my own life, he is also the Vicar of Christ, which can suffice for every Christian to make him walk in his service
with the same fidelity and truth that he would with the Lord himself, who sees the inmost depths [f. 385v] of our hearts.
Therefore, when Our Lord finds in me — I do not say the enormous and execrable failing of having had dealings with the
ambassador of England, whom I neither know nor ever, to my knowledge, have seen, as I am advised and as is written to
the King himself to have been said to Our Lord — but any other least failing that I may have committed through malice
in his service, I beg him to have no pity or mercy on me, but to punish me with the [harshest] and severest punishments
that can be given to the most wicked man in the world. [But] I, if I am not mistaken, would believe that neither with
Your Most Illustrious Lordship nor with Our Lord ought anyone to have had more trust than I, since there is no one more
obliged to him; besides which I believe that, by the grace of the Lord God, I have been known by all who have had
dealings with me to be utterly removed from the vice of ingratitude; and when Your Most Illustrious Lordship chooses to
test my fidelity and gratitude, you will find that you have no one in this world on whom you can have more […]

R48, Francia 22/27, Blois, 30 & 31 Jan 1589

Morosini again asks for his leave. The Parisians have put themselves under Mayenne's protection, and the King is leaving for Amboise with his prisoners. Morosini protests about moving the Cardinal de Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon.
