# R57 — English (Morosini to Montalto, [Moulins, June 1589]: two French papers sent to M. de la Guiche, in Italian translation)

Translation of `R57_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 524r] [For] Your Most Illustrious Lordship […] translation of the letter written to Monsieur de la Guiche.

My lord, while I was looking for an express messenger to send you, I found this bearer, a messenger from Moulins, who
promised me to come and see you and give you the present letter, by which I shall let you know the happy outcome of my
journey so far, thanks be to God, with very good news, which I hope, by the grace of God, to bring to the King, better
than he expected. His army of Swiss [?…] four leagues from Montbéliard […] now that […] left […] will be at Langres […]
this month at the latest; they number thirteen thousand Swiss, two thousand landsknechts and 1,500 reiters; the rest
are French; in all they may be seventeen to eighteen thousand men, with […] twelve pieces of artillery. It is a strange
thing, the credit of His Majesty and the great offers of men and money made to him: the city of Strasbourg alone
[has] lent […] thousand scudi, out of which Monsieur de Sancy has paid [?6,000] reiters and twelve thousand Swiss who
will follow this army for six weeks. I found Signor Cesare [?at] Semur and in the […], to whom I said what he must do
in passing through the county, because […] is holding out for the League, [which] runs a great risk. I gave him a
passport and showed him what [f. 524v] he must do. The said Swiss are coming to Langres, and from there I believe
they will pass by [?the] gates of Dijon, and from there to Autun, [and] Decize. This [?10th] day of June 1589. Your
more than most humble and most obedient servant, Regnault.

[…] translation of the oath taken by those of the town of Moulins on this day, 16 June 1589, in the presence of
Monsieur de la Guiche, councillor of the King in his privy council of state, grand master of the artillery of France
and lieutenant [?general] for His Majesty in his army of foreigners, of Swiss. The consuls and échevins, residents and
inhabitants of the town and [fau]bourgs of Moulins in the Bourbonnais, assembled in the castle of Moulins, have
unanimously made and taken the oath of fidelity to the King our sire Henri the Third, by the grace of God King of
France and of Poland, and in the hands of Monsieur de Chazeron, lieutenant general for His Majesty in the [government]
of the said country, and have promised on their faith, life and honour, and on their loyalty and conscience, to live
and die in the Catholic, apostolic and Roman religion, under the obedience of His Majesty, and not to depart from it in
any way, nor to undertake or favour, in any way whatever, the enemies of his state and person, and to remain his
faithful [f. 525r] subjects and most humble servants, [and] to [?…] it and defend it towards and against all, he being
their legitimate and sovereign king, and to obey the commands that shall be given them, whether by Monsieur de
Chazeron or other lieutenants general of His Majesty, for his service; and to this effect they have renounced and
withdrawn from all promises and associations they may have made to the contrary, if there are any. In witness whereof
those of the said inhabitants who can sign have signed, and as regards those who cannot sign, they have given their
names, which have been transcribed by the notary of the lordship of Bourbonnais at the end of these presents. […]

R58, Francia 22/37, Moulins, 5 July 1589 (dup.)

The King has taken Jargeau ("Giorgio") and its Loire bridge, hanged a captain and pardoned the governor. Other Loire towns have surrendered, and the King is heading for Paris, where four faubourgs are said to favour him. Mayenne has taken Montereau and Nemours is raising money at Lyon for the League's Swiss.

# R58 — Morosini to Montalto, Moulins, 5 July 1589: Jargeau taken, the King's march on Paris (Francia 22/37, ff. 533r–534r)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription D1722 (KaJo) under Meister no. 40, segmented into words by
`research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R58_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every break re-parsed by hand on
the transcribed figures (`R58_corrections.tsv`). The sheet is headed in clear (DECODE): "Molins à li v di Luglio 1589.
dup.lo" (a duplicate). The three DECODE "cleartext" images are clear despatches, not a decipherment. Not in Tempesti.
Numbers in plain figures between null 8s (30 [milia], 25 [milia]). Place names as the clerk wrote them: Giorgio
(Jargeau), Gian (Gien), Loira, Orliens, Nantes, Pluuiers (Pithiviers), Etampes, Montereo (Montereau), Ciamberi
(Chambéry), Ouernia (Auvergne), Meos (Meaux), Longauila (Longueville). Spelling as the figures give it; punctuation,
capitals and word division added; codes expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 129 duca di, 143 guerra, 146 danari,
151 Francia, 165/166 quello/questo, 167 V. S. Ill.ma, 216 auisi, 221 lettere, 227 heretici). Marks: [?word] partly
carried, […] unread.

## Reading

[f. 533r] […] questo […] dele cose di qui, io non lasarò di dirle quello che s'intende, se bene con molta dificoltà si
può sapere una uerità, poiché ognuno parla secondo il suo senso. Si è inteso che il Re habia preso Giorgio, hauendo
quei di dentro aspetato il canone prima che uolersi rendere; et perché il logo è debolisimo, se bene d'importanza per
hauere un ponte di pietra sul fiume dela Loira et per esere quatro sole leghe lontano da Orliens, dicono che S. M.tà
non habia uoluto acetar loro alcuna conditione, ma liberam[ente] a sua discretione; con tuto ciò l'ha preseruato dal
saco, non senza molta dificoltà et mala sodisfatione de' soldati, che, non esendo pagati, sperauano almeno di
guadagnare qual[che] cosa in quella ocasione. Entrata [?…] S. M.tà con i principali caualieri che sono seco, ha fato
impicare un capitano che fu incolpato d'esere stato quello che haueua persuasi i popoli a non si rendere, et di farli
abrusciare un borgo di fuori per leuare la comodità da alogiamenti al esercito, oltre che questo capitano poco tempo
prima haueua tochi danari per fare gente in seruitio del Re, et nondimeno, da poi riceuti, si era uoltato in fauore
dela lega. Haueua anco S. M.tà condanato nela medesma pena il gouernatore di quella tera; ma, condoto al logo del
suplicio, hauendo diuersi signori intercesso per lui con dire che era bon soldato et che nel auenire hauria seruito a
S. M.tà, […] il perdonò; ma però si tiene tutauia prigione. Ha anco S. M.tà fato carcerare alcuni de' principali dela
tera per hauere danari. S'intende che quello di Gian, tera dieci leghe discosta da Giorgio, doue è un altro ponte di
pietra sopra il fiume dela Loira, ueduto che il Re s'apresaua a quella uolta, haueuano inuiato a dimandare socorso al
sig. duca di Umena; ma non l'hauendo hauto, senza aspetare l'esercito haueano inuiato a rendersi a S. M.tà, come fano
quasi tute l'altre tere di quei contorni, che non si posono [f. 533v] longam[ente] tenire, la quale li haueua
amoreuolm[ente] riceuti. Nel medesmo tempo dicono che il Nauarro haueua con inganno preso Pluuiers, et oue si era
incaminata S. M.tà, che hora si ritroua padrona di tuti i ponti che sono sopra la Loira, da Orliens et Nantes in poi;
et dicono che sia risoluta d'andare diritam[ente] uerso Parigi. Per doue dicesi che sono anco incaminati li suoi
suizeri, che di nuouo uengono incontro, ai quali haueua S. M.tà inuiato il duca di Longauila in iscambio di mons. dela
Guiscia, che era prima stato destinato a questa carica et partito ancora con buona compagnia; ma due giorni dopo hebe
lettere del Re con le quali gli comandaua di ritornarsene in queste parti del Borbonese, dicendo che presto gli
inuiar[i]a gente per fare la guerra in Ouernia contra quelli dela lega. Si dice da altra parte che il duca di Umena
haueua ripreso Montereo et anco castelo […], et che s'incaminaua per andare a combatere li suizeri del Re prima che si
posino unire con S. M.tà, et che mons. di Nemours usaua ogni diligenza a Lione per hauere danari per dare ai suizeri
che uengono in seruitio dela lega, ne li quali dicono esere giunti a Ciamberi in numero di undici milia, tuta buona
gente, la quale non uole pasare oltre se non le uengono dati danari; ma che subito [?hauuti] s'incaminarano per la
Borgogna ala coda de gl'altri suizeri heretici per combaterli. Gli afetionati del Re dicono che S. M.tà ha, senza li
suizeri et raitri, 30 milia persone in esere, et che il sig. duca di Umena ha pochisima gente; et gli afetionati dela
lega dicono che egli ha più di 25 milia persone, et che il Re non ne ha sei milia, et che i suizeri heretici, che gli
altri dicono che […] molto inanzi, non hano ancora trouata uia per entrare in Francia. Onde io non saprei che
afermare a V. S. Ill.ma, se bene io [f. 534r] ho parlato con uno del duca di Niuers, che mi dice hauere lui medesmo
lasato i sodeti suizeri a Langres già molti giorni; ma egli ancora potria dire il falso. In questo punto è uenuto a
uedermi mons. di Forges, che partì mercordì pasato da Pluuiers, [?doue] dice che il medesmo giorno era anco partito il
Re per Etampes, hauendo hauto auisi dal Nauarro che i borghi di quella tera erano tuti per S. M.tà, et che già
haueuano anco guadagnata la fosa et piantata l'artigliaria, intanto che sperauano molto presto di hauere la tera. Dice
anco che quatro de i borghi di Parigi, cioè san Marceo, san Uitor, san Iaches et san Germano, haueuano fato sapere a
S. M.tà che teniuano per lei, et che, uolendo andare a quella uolta, che loro l'hauriano molto alegram[ente] riceuuta;
et che per questo rispeto, subito che sarà terminata l'impresa di Etampes, senza aspetare più longam[ente] i
stranieri, il Re col suo esercito s'incaminarà a quella uolta, intendendosi che il duca di Umena era a Meos un poco
amalato. Referisce ancora che il conte di Soisone, che era prigione nel castelo di Nantes, si era saluato con metersi
in una cesta, nela quale soleuano portargli il mangiare in castelo: cosa asai dificile da credere. Non ho uoluto lasare
di dire a V. S. Ill.ma quello che questo mons. mi ha referto, se bene io gli presto poca fede, esendo molto partiale
seruitore del Re. [?Adeso] certo che uiene dala corte, hauendomi [p]ortate lettere del sig. Galeazo Fregoso, et dele
nuoue si rimete a quello che intenderò da eso mons., non mi è parso douer lasare di darne conto a V. S. Ill.ma, che le
meterà in quella consideratione che parerà ala singolar sua prudenza. […]

# R58 — English (Morosini to Montalto, Moulins, 5 July 1589: Jargeau taken, the King's march on Paris)

Translation of `R58_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 533r] […] this […] of things here, I shall not fail to tell you what is heard, although one can learn the truth only
with great difficulty, since everyone speaks according to his own feeling. It is heard that the King has taken Jargeau,
those inside having waited for the cannon before being willing to surrender; and because the place is very weak,
though important for having a stone bridge over the river Loire and for being only four leagues from Orléans, they say
His Majesty would accept no conditions from them, only [surrender] freely at his discretion; nevertheless he saved it
from the sack, not without much difficulty and the displeasure of the soldiers, who, not being paid, hoped at least to
gain something on that occasion. [Having entered] […] with the principal knights who are with him, His Majesty has had a
captain hanged who was accused of having persuaded the people not to surrender, and had a suburb outside burned, to
take away the convenience of quarters from the army; besides, this captain had shortly before received money to raise
men in the King's service, and nevertheless, after receiving it, had turned to the League's side. His Majesty had also
condemned the governor of that town to the same penalty; but when he had been brought to the place of execution, and
several lords had interceded for him, saying he was a good soldier and would in future serve His Majesty, […] pardoned
him; but he is still kept prisoner. His Majesty has also had some of the principal men of the town jailed to get money.
It is heard that those of Gien, a town ten leagues from Jargeau, where there is another stone bridge over the Loire,
seeing the King approaching, had sent to ask help of the Lord Duke of Mayenne; but not having had it, without waiting
for the army they had sent to surrender to His Majesty, as almost all the other towns round about do, which cannot
[f. 533v] hold out long; and he had received them kindly. At the same time they say that Navarre had taken Pithiviers by
a ruse, and that His Majesty had set out there; he now finds himself master of all the bridges on the Loire, Orléans
and Nantes apart; and they say he is resolved to go straight towards Paris. It is said that his Swiss are also on the
way there, who are coming to meet him again; to whom His Majesty had sent the Duke of Longueville in place of Monsieur
de la Guiche, who had first been appointed to this charge and had already set out with a good company; but two days
later he had letters [from the] King ordering him to return to these parts of the Bourbonnais, saying that he would
soon send him men to make war in Auvergne against those of the League. It is said from the other side that the Duke of
Mayenne had retaken Montereau and also castle […], and that he was on his way to fight the King's Swiss before they
could join His Majesty, and that Monsieur de Nemours was making every effort at Lyon to get money to give to the Swiss
coming in the League's service, of whom they say eleven thousand have reached Chambéry, all good troops, who will not
go further unless they are given money; but that as soon as [they have it] they will set out through Burgundy on the
tail of the other, heretic, Swiss to fight them. The King's supporters say that His Majesty has, without the Swiss and
reiters, 30,000 men in being, and that the Lord Duke of Mayenne has very few troops; and the League's supporters say
that he has more than 25,000 men and the King not six thousand, and that the heretic Swiss, who others say […] well
ahead, have not yet found a way to enter France. So I would not know what to affirm to Your Most Illustrious Lordship,
although I [f. 534r] have spoken with one of the Duke of Nevers's men, who tells me he himself left the said Swiss at
Langres many days ago; but he too might be saying what is false. At this moment Monsieur de Forges has come to see me,
who left Pithiviers last Wednesday, [where] he says the King had also left the same day for Étampes, having had word
from Navarre that the suburbs of that town were all for His Majesty and that they had already won the ditch and
planted the artillery, so that they hoped to have the town very soon. He also says that four of the suburbs of Paris,
namely Saint-Marceau, Saint-Victor, Saint-Jacques and Saint-Germain, had let His Majesty know that they held for him,
and that if he wished to go that way they would receive him very gladly; and that for this reason, as soon as the
enterprise of Étampes is finished, without waiting longer for the foreigners, the King will march that way with his
army, it being understood that the Duke of Mayenne was at Meaux, somewhat ill. He reports further that the Count of
Soissons, who was a prisoner in the castle of Nantes, had escaped by putting himself in a basket in which they used to
carry his food into the castle: a thing very hard to believe. I did not want to fail to tell Your Most Illustrious
Lordship what this monsieur has reported to me, although I give him little credit, being a very partial servant of the
King. [?Now] certain [news] coming from the court, having brought me letters from Signor Galeazzo Fregoso, and he
referring for the news to what I shall hear from the said monsieur, it did not seem to me I should fail to give an
account of it to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, who will give it the consideration your singular prudence thinks fit.
[…]

A Morosini-period letter of 1587 in the Meister no. 40 key, filed by DECODE with the Bergamo/Nazareth despatches: it concerns the Duke of Lorraine and Guise, the German reiters, the Queen Mother and Schomberg.

# R17 — Nuncio's cipher enclosure, Paris, 1586–87: the Duke of Lorraine's army and the oath (Francia 18/3, ff. 233r, 234r–235v)

Rests on: the figures. DECODE's transcription (TimB, Dec 2015, `R17_transcription_decode.txt`) under Meister no. 40,
segmented into words by `research/reading_audit/reread_b00_decode.py` (`R17_worddecode.txt`, `_figs.txt`), then every
break re-parsed by hand on the transcribed figures and, where a figure itself was in doubt, on the DECODE images (crops;
`R17_corrections.tsv`). No contemporary decipherment on the DECODE images: the two "cleartext" images (ff. 231r, 232r)
are covering letters in clear signed by the archbishop of Nazareth (Fabio Mirto Frangipani), Paris 27 August 1586 and
27 July 1586; the cipher is not dated. Its content (the King's call to the dukes of Lorraine and Guise, revoked on
Épernon's advice; Schomberg and Bellièvre sent to the Duke of Lorraine over the oath of his troops; the Queen Mother
fearing war among Catholics) fits 1587 (DECODE dates the record 1585–88). The writer is the nuncio ("io non ho mancato
di dar animo a la Regina Madre").
Page order: 233r, then 234r–235v. 233v is not imaged and 234r begins in mid-sentence, so 233r and 234r may not be
consecutive; 235v ends in mid-sentence (the rest is not in the record).
Spelling as the figures give it (single for double consonants); punctuation, capitals and word division added; codes
expanded (113 S. M.tà / il Re, 111 N. S., 116 Regina Madre, 129 duca di, 146 danari, 151 Francia, 161 quanto,
165/166 quello/questo in the form needed, 217 corriere, 221 lettere, 226 catolici, 227 heretici).
Marks: [?word] partly carried, […] unread, [word] supplied.

## Reading

[f. 233r] […] per procurare di leuare le dificultà et difidentie et introdure l'unione, che sola può giouare ai
presenti bisogni […].

[…] il marsciale di Res, che teme asai questi acidenti, in un longo ragionamento che ha fato meco hogi conclude che,
se N. S., come padre dela christianità, non interpone uiuamente l'autorità sua così con il Re come anco con gli altri,
non uede rimedio che questo regno non si perda. Onde io, per intendere quello che egli uolese dire che potese in
questo caso fare la Santità di N. S., dopo longo circuito di parole dise che questo era ricercare d'intendere le
pretensioni del'una et l'altra parte, dar la ragione et il torto a che l'hauese, procurando poi con la soprema sua
autorità di fare che ognuno si contenti del honesto; et che non c'era altro rimedio a questo male.

[f. 234r] […] come […] quanto era stata grande l'alegreza che tuti i buoni haueano sentito dela risolutione fata dal Re
di chiamare il duca di Loreno e quello di Guisa con le loro forze ad unirsi con la M.tà S., tanto anco è stato magiore
il dispiacere che si è sentito dela mutatione fata da S. M.tà, la quale, per quanto si dice, haueua presa la prima
deliberatione con il parere del suo consiglio, in tempo però che mons. di Epernone non c'era presente, esendo alhora
andato con una grosa banda di gente per tentare di fare qualche [?danno] a' inimici. Ma esendo egli ritornato et
intendendo di questo ordine già ispedito, ha saputo tanto dire che ha persuaso S. M.tà a riuocarlo, cometendo esa
perciò con lettere di propria mano al marsciale di Res che, se bene per altre spedite a lui dala segretaria lo
comandaua d'andare con le genti ch'ha seco ad unirsi con il duca di Guisa, nondimeno si guardi molto bene, per quanto
ha cara la uita, di farlo; e per disturbare anco la uenuta del duca di Loreno spedì a la uolta sua un gentil'ho[f. 234v]mo,
rinouando la dificoltà, di già acomodata, del giuramento, con dire [?che], quando egli uoglia che tute le sue genti lo
prestino, deba restar sei me[si in] suo paese. Al che eso signore duca rispose che, et per il primo ordine che S. M.tà
gli diede d'andarlo a ritrouare, et per il protesto mandatogli a fare dopo per mons. di Sciumbergh, che se in questo
suo bisogno non andasero tute le sue genti a socorerla si saria doluta di lui, et che egli perciò, et per dimostrare
ancora l'afetione et diuotione che portaua a S. M.tà, haueua con molto interese trouati danari per pagare le sue genti,
come ha già fato, et per andarla a seruire; che ela non haueua ragione di domandare giuramento a le genti pagate da
lui, douendole bastare quello che lui steso faria a la S. M.tà; che però egli era risoluto di uenire in ogni modo. Et
esendo di questa risposta rimasto il Re malisimo sodisfato, ha con duo corieri, l'uno apreso al'altro, [f. 235r]
replicato al sodeto duca che non deba entrare in Francia; ma non potendo con tuto ciò rimouerlo, stando egli fermo di
uolere in ogni modo [uenire], esendo di già pasato tanto inanzi che si troua a […] leghe lontano di qu[i], gli ha di
nuouo spedito S. M.tà un protesto che, se uenirà più oltre et non si ritirarà fuori del suo regno, uoltarà contra di lui
tuti questi eserciti; né ancora si sa se questo haurà a bastare per fare che si ritorni. Di che [?la] Regina Madre sta
con molto trauaglio, temendo [?che] non segua qualche inconueniente iremediabile, et però gli ha spedito hieri mons. di
Beleure, pregandolo con grandisima instanza a uolere dare ogni sodisfatione al Re, o col fare prestar il giuramento
dale sue genti a S. M.tà, ouero col ritornarsene nel suo paese; et hora si sta aspetando la sua risposta, la quale, se
sarà che in ogni modo uoglia uenire [f. 235v] senza il giuramento, si tiene per sicuro che il Re sia per uoltare le
sue forze contra di lui, tenendo per certo che l'intentione sua et degli altri dela lega sia uolta a leuarsi la corona;
et di già si discorre da persone di molta qualità che posa uenire a Parigi con intentione di far ridure un consiglio
deli tre Stati del regno per dichiarare il Re inhabile al gouerno. Il che, se bene non pare uerisimile in tempo che si
trouano tanti heretici nel regno, nondimeno la Regina Madre, nel ragionamento che ho hauto hogi seco, ha dimostrato di
temere asai, se continua il duca di Loreno a uoler uenire inanzi, di qualche infelice suceso. Io non ho mancato di dar
animo a la Regina Madre, et se uedrò che si uada a camino di combatere fra catolici, non lasciarò di fare tuto quello
che sarà in me per impedirlo, come non pretermeto anco al presente di fare tuti quelli ufici che io po[…]

## Notes on the figures

- 233r l. 1: "4 5 1 9 1 8" before "per procurare" (s o + null) is the end of a word from a page not in the record.
- 233r l. 4: "8 0 0 4 4 5 7 0" closes the paragraph before a drawn line; it does not parse (checked on the image).
- 233r l. 5: "7 0 5 1 4 9 2 1 1 5 0 0 8" before "il maresciale" does not parse into words (checked on the image).
- "Onde io" (233r l. 11): figures 8 9 0 1 2 6 5 1 7 1 9 = (null 8) o n d e, io; the 9 is on the image (r2p, 23 Oct 2026), so onde is carried.
- "dar la ragione" (233r l. 16): 2 6 2 6 2 1 1 8 = d (d) a r + null; one 26 doubled.
- 234r l. 1: "0 2 7 9 5 0 1 6^. 6 4 1 0 8" before "quanto era stata": m, come (79), then a dotted 166 and figures that
  do not parse; the sentence needs no more than "come … quanto … tanto".
- "qualche [?danno]" (234r l. 11): figures 3 8 2 6 3 1 0 1 9 (d . n n o with a 3 where a 21 is wanted).
- "di questo ordine" (234r l. 12): "1 1^. 6 6 9 0 0 2 6 1 7 0 1 1 5 3" is 166 with the dot on the wrong figure, then
  o r d i n e; the decoder had read it as 116 (Regina Madre).
- "[?che]" (234v l. 2): the figures give 63 (chi) before 99 (quando).
- "me[si in] suo paese" (234v l. 4): 2 0 5 4 3 7 9 = m e, s u o; the end of mesi and a preposition are not written.
- "Sciumbergh" (234v l. 8): 4 5 5 2 1 7 3 7 0 2 2 4 3 5 0 0 0 4 1 4 = Gaspard de Schomberg; a stray 2 precedes it.
- "trouati danari per" (234v l. 13): 1 4 6 6 4 = 146 (danari) written without its dot, then 64 per.
- "a […] leghe" (235r l. 5): "1 8 8 4 9 0 0 3 5 1 5 3" (a number in plain figures, 18?, and s o r e) does not parse.
- "[?la] Regina Madre" (235r l. 11): figures 5 2 1 2 before 116; la would be 50 212.
- "[?che] non segua" (235r l. 12): figures 6 3 (chi) again where che is wanted.
- "tanti heretici" (235v l. 11): 2^. 2 7 = 227 with the dot on the first figure.

# R17 — English (nuncio's cipher enclosure, Paris, 1586–87: the Duke of Lorraine's army and the oath)

Translation of `R17_reading.md`; holes as there.

## Translation

[f. 233r] […] to try to remove the difficulties and mistrust and to bring in union, which alone can help the present
needs […].

[…] the Maréchal de Retz, who greatly fears these events, concludes, in a long conversation he had with me today, that
unless Our Lord, as father of Christendom, interposes his authority vigorously both with the King and with the others,
he sees no remedy to keep this kingdom from being lost. [So] I, to understand what he meant that His Holiness could do
in this case — after a long circuit of words he said that this meant seeking to understand the claims of
the one party and the other, giving right and wrong to whoever had it, and then working, with his supreme authority, to
make everyone content with what is fair; and that there was no other remedy for this evil.

[f. 234r] […] as […] great as was the joy that all good men had felt at the resolution taken by the King to call the
Duke of Lorraine and the Duke of Guise with their forces to join His Majesty, so much greater has been the displeasure
felt at the change made by His Majesty. He had taken the first decision, so it is said, with the advice of his council,
but at a time when Monsieur d'Épernon was not present, having then gone with a large band of men to try to do the
enemy some [harm]. But when he returned and learned of this order, already sent out, he managed to say so much that he
persuaded His Majesty to revoke it; and His Majesty therefore ordered the Maréchal de Retz by letters in his own hand
that, although by other letters sent to him from the secretariat he had been commanded to go with the troops he has with
him to join the Duke of Guise, he should nonetheless take great care, as he values his life, not to do it. And to hinder
the coming of the Duke of Lorraine as well, he sent a gentleman [f. 234v] to him, renewing the difficulty, already
settled, about the oath, saying [that] if he wishes all his troops to take it, he must stay six months [in] his own
country. To which the said Lord Duke answered that, both because of the first order His Majesty gave him to come and
join him, and because of the protest sent to him afterwards through Monsieur de Schomberg (that if in this need of hers
all his troops did not go to her help she would have cause to complain of him), and also to show his affection and
devotion to His Majesty, he had at great cost found money to pay his troops, as he has already done, and to go and
serve her; that she had no reason to ask an oath of troops paid by him, since what he himself would give to Her Majesty
should suffice; and that he was therefore resolved to come in any case. The King, very ill satisfied with this answer,
has [f. 235r] sent two couriers, one after the other, to repeat to the said Duke that he must not enter France. But
being unable even so to move him, since he stands firm in wishing to [come] in any case and has already advanced so far
that he is […] leagues from here, His Majesty has again sent him a protest that, if he comes any further and does not
withdraw out of his kingdom, he will turn all these armies against him; and it is not yet known whether this will be
enough to make him turn back. [At this] the Queen Mother is in great distress, fearing [that] some irremediable mishap
may follow, and so yesterday she sent Monsieur de Bellièvre to him, begging him most urgently to give the King every
satisfaction, either by having his troops take the oath to His Majesty or by returning to his own country. His answer is
now awaited; and if it is that he wants to come in any case [f. 235v] without the oath, it is held for certain that the
King will turn his forces against him, being sure that his intention, and that of the others of the League, is aimed at
taking the crown for themselves. And people of great standing are already saying that he might come to Paris intending
to have a council of the three Estates of the kingdom assembled to declare the King unfit to govern. Although this does
not seem likely at a time when there are so many heretics in the kingdom, nonetheless the Queen Mother, in the
conversation I had with her today, showed that she greatly fears some unhappy outcome if the Duke of Lorraine goes on
wishing to advance. I have not failed to encourage the Queen Mother, and if I see that things are heading towards
fighting among Catholics I shall not fail to do all that is in me to prevent it, as I do not omit even now to do all
those offices that I can […]

06 Sources
